Finding (SPEC 1d-ii). The raw sediment-exposure toxicity doses in ToMEx (dose.particles.kg.sediment.master) span a physically plausible particles/kg-dry-weight range (tens to ~10^10), consistent with the order of magnitude of Redondo-Hasselerharm et al. (2023)’s benthic HC5 (4.9×10⁹ particles/kg dw). No hardcoded water-to-sediment unit-conversion factor (e.g., a missing bulk-density or dry-weight scalar) was found in the dose_unit = "kg" code path: run_pssd_pipeline(..., dose_unit = "kg") (R/mp_risk_utils.R) selects the particles_kg_food_dilution/particles_kg_ox_stress columns from PSSDplusplus::MC_sim_align_parallel()’s output, which in turn are populated directly from each sediment study’s own reported particles/kg dose (via align_data()’s dose.particles.kg.master coalescing chain), not derived from a water-based value. The hazard side therefore appears to be genuinely unit-consistent on its own terms. The implausibly low derived sediment Food Dilution HC5 (exact value in the guard below) cannot be attributed to a discrete missing-conversion bug found in this trace; it is more likely size-alignment sensitivity to the sediment ERM exponents (the same mechanism SPEC 1b addressed for Food Dilution) for whichever study anchors the low tail, amplified by SSD-extrapolation noise on a modest sediment toxicity dataset (89 records). This remains an open question rather than a resolved code fix, since (unlike SPEC 1d-i) no single incorrect line was identified. Regardless, because the exposure-side concentration is already known to be non-quantitative, this hazard-side question does not change the conclusion that the sediment RQ/HC5 below must be excluded from the headline risk characterization.

A FAIL here is EXPECTED and is additional confirmation that the current sediment pathway must not be reported as a real risk finding.

The current derived sediment Food Dilution HC5 fails the plausibility guard above by roughly eleven orders of magnitude (see the rendered value; expected to be on the order of 0.0002 particles/kg vs. a published benthic range of 10¹-10¹² particles/kg dw), consistent with the SPEC 1d-i finding that the sediment pathway’s exposure concentration is not a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight value. The sediment Food Dilution and Tissue Translocation RQ/HC5 figures in this report are illustrative/non-quantitative and are excluded from the headline risk characterization (Sections 14-15) pending a genuine dry-weight sediment concentration.

11.5 Sediment as a time-dependent, accumulating compartment

Rationale. Sediment is an accumulating, long-residence depositional compartment, and it is the sink for the large/dense particles that differential settling removes from the water column (Hoffman et al. 2026; the critical-size capture-fraction diagnostic in Section 13 quantifies that filtering mechanism for this dataset). Those deposited particles continue to fragment in situ, so — per Thuy-Dung, Groenenberg & Koelmans (2026) — both exposure (bioaccessible particle number) and hazard (HC5, via which benthic species are size-accessible) are dynamic rather than static. A single-time-point sediment RQ is therefore a snapshot that can under-represent future risk in an accumulating bed. Everything in this section is a framework upgrade, not a live risk calculation: the sediment exposure concentration remains non-quantitative (sediment_concentration_is_quantitative = FALSE, SPEC 1d), so nothing here re-introduces sediment into the headline risk conclusion (Sections 11.3.0/11.4.0/15.3).

11.5.1 Temporal fragmentation framing

  • Sediment is treated as a time-dependent, accumulating compartment. Deposited microplastics continue to fragment, shifting the particle-size distribution toward smaller, more numerous, more bioaccessible particles over residence time in the bed.
  • Consequently, any static sediment metric is a lower-bound snapshot. Both HC5 (which benthic species are size-accessible) and bioaccessible exposure evolve as fragmentation proceeds — the single-time-point Food Dilution/Tissue Translocation figures in Section 11.4 describe the sediment PSD’s condition at the time of sampling, not its trajectory.
  • This compounds, rather than substitutes for, the SPEC 1d exposure-concentration problem. Even once a genuine dry-weight sediment concentration becomes available, a single power-law fit to that concentration would still understate risk relative to the bed’s future, more-fragmented state.
  • Cite Thuy-Dung, Groenenberg & Koelmans (2026) — a prospective, temporally-explicit risk framework for fragmenting microplastics (size-independent fragmentation rate constant kfrag, doubling time TD) in which HC5 and RCR are time-dependent because shrinking particles become bioaccessible to progressively more sensitive species; the source paper’s median HC5 example drops from 2.1×10⁴ to 1.95×10³ particles/kg when a sensitive species becomes accessible, and individual-species RCR>1 can precede a derivable community SSD by roughly a decade. Cross-reference: the Hoffman et al. (2026) differential-settling sink argument already used in this document (Section 13’s critical-size diagnostic) is the mechanism that puts large/dense particles into the sediment bed in the first place; SPEC 1e is about what happens to them after they arrive.

11.5.3 Time-varying bioaccessibility (documented; future enhancement)

Making the existing pSSD++ bioaccessibility size-gate explicitly time-dependent (HC5(t)/RCR(t) as a trajectory) is deferred: it needs a residence-time/age-of-deposition axis that does not exist in the source sediment dataset. Full scoping in Appendix C.

11.5.4 Most-sensitive-species screen (sediment)

Per Thuy-Dung et al. (2026), individual-species risk can precede a derivable community SSD signal by roughly a decade, and the sediment benthic SSD here is small and comparatively unstable (89 records, 9 species). This screen identifies the single most sensitive species (lowest aligned effect dose) per ERM and reports it alongside the community HC5 already computed in Section 11.4 — as an early-warning companion, not a replacement.

For Food Dilution, the single most sensitive species among the 7 sediment benthic species considered is Chironomus tepperi (median aligned dose = 0.00441 particles/kg dw, 30000 aligned records), compared with the community Food Dilution HC5 of 0.000248 particles/kg dw computed in Section 11.4. For Tissue Translocation, the most sensitive species is Chironomus tepperi (median aligned dose = 79.9 particles/kg dw, 30000 records), compared with the community Tissue Translocation HC5 of 4.65 particles/kg dw. As Section 11.5.3 notes, a finer PSD from continued fragmentation could bring additional, potentially more sensitive species into bioaccessible range over time, which is part of why this individual-species screen is worth tracking alongside the community HC5 rather than assuming the current community SSD is stable. This screen does not change the sediment exclusion from the headline conclusion (its inputs are the same non-quantitative-exposure sediment pathway); the companion individual-species screen for the quantitative river/ocean water compartments is reported in Section 15.4, once every matrix’s hazard objects have been computed.

12. Ocean Water

Ocean water samples were collected from the coastal/marine environment and analyzed using the same µFTIR workflow as river water. Marine species are evaluated using the PSSDplusplus marine toxicity endpoints and alignment parameters, which characterize exposure and hazard in particles/L rather than particles/kg (sediment).

12.1 Particle data and C-PSD fitting

Particle volume computation

Show the code 
# Compute W/L thickness ratio from ocean particles (same instrument as river)
ratio_tbl_ocean <- raw_particles_ocean |>
  dplyr::mutate(WL = 1 / aspect_ratio) |>
  dplyr::group_by(shape) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n      = dplyr::n(),
    r_med  = median(WL, na.rm = TRUE),
    r_low  = quantile(WL, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    r_high = quantile(WL, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

raw_particles_ocean <- raw_particles_ocean |>
  assign_polymer_density(lookup = polymer_density_tbl) |>
  dplyr::left_join(ratio_tbl_ocean |> dplyr::select(shape, r_med), by = "shape") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    height_um = r_med * width_um,
    V_um3 = dplyr::case_when(
      shape == "fragment" ~ (pi / 6) * length_um * width_um * height_um,
      shape == "fiber"    ~ pi * (width_um / 2)^2 * length_um,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    ),
    mass_ug = V_um3 * density_g_cm3,
    mass_ug_fixed_density_1.1 = V_um3 * 1.1
  )

cat("Ocean particles: n =", nrow(raw_particles_ocean),

# Ocean-water sample_location carries the same four river-mouth-adjacent
# coastal site names as raw_particles_river (Carmel, Pajaro, Salinas, San
# Lorenzo) -- ocean water was collected adjacent to each river's discharge,
# not at one generic offshore site -- so the same per-location C-PSD fit and
# heterogeneity test used for river water (Section 4.2.4) can be run here.
# Ocean per-location n is much smaller than river (117 total vs 1207), so a
# tryCatch guard (mirroring safe_cpsd() in Section 4.2.4) is required: some
# locations may have too few/too sparse particles for the two-step LOD
# algorithm to find any valid populated-bin window.
ocean_locations <- sort(unique(raw_particles_ocean$sample_location))

safe_cpsd_ocean_loc <- function(data, ...) {
  if (length(data) < 10) return(list(valid = FALSE))
  tryCatch(
    c(fit_cpsd_segur_r(data, ...), list(valid = TRUE)),
    error = function(e) list(valid = FALSE)
  )
}

cpsd_fits_ocean_by_loc <- lapply(setNames(ocean_locations, ocean_locations), function(loc) {
  dat <- raw_particles_ocean |> dplyr::filter(sample_location == loc) |> dplyr::pull(length_um)
  safe_cpsd_ocean_loc(dat, bin_um = 5)
})

ocean_loc_summary <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(cpsd_fits_ocean_by_loc), function(loc) {
  fo <- cpsd_fits_ocean_by_loc[[loc]]
  if (isTRUE(fo$valid)) {
    tibble::tibble(
      location     = loc,
      n_particles  = sum(raw_particles_ocean$sample_location == loc),
      a_cpsd       = round(fo$a_cpsd,   3),
      se_a_cpsd    = round(fo$se_a_cpsd, 3),
      a_psd        = round(fo$a_psd,    3),
      lod_low_um   = round(fo$lower_lod_used_um, 0),
      lod_high_um  = round(fo$upper_lod_um,       0),
      r2           = round(fo$r2,       3),
      n_bins       = fo$n_bins,
      fit_mode     = fo$fit_mode
    )
  } else {
    tibble::tibble(
      location = loc, n_particles = sum(raw_particles_ocean$sample_location == loc),
      a_cpsd = NA_real_, se_a_cpsd = NA_real_, a_psd = NA_real_,
      lod_low_um = NA_real_, lod_high_um = NA_real_, r2 = NA_real_,
      n_bins = NA_integer_, fit_mode = "no_fit"
    )
  }
}))

# Same Cochran's Q heterogeneity test as the river-location version above,
# applied to the ocean per-location slopes. Locations with fit_mode != "ok"
# (too few particles/bins for a valid LOD window) are excluded from the test

ocean_slope_heterogeneity <- if (nrow(ocean_loc_summary_valid) >= 2) {
  slope_heterogeneity_test(
    a = ocean_loc_summary_valid$a_cpsd, se = ocean_loc_summary_valid$se_a_cpsd,
    labels = ocean_loc_summary_valid$location
  )
} else NULL

if (!is.null(ocean_slope_heterogeneity)) {
  cat(
    "Ocean (coastal) location slope heterogeneity: Q(", ocean_slope_heterogeneity$df, ") = ",
    round(ocean_slope_heterogeneity$Q, 2), ", p = ", signif(ocean_slope_heterogeneity$p_value, 3),
    ", I2 = ", round(ocean_slope_heterogeneity$i2, 1), "%, weighted-mean a_cpsd = ",
    round(ocean_slope_heterogeneity$weighted_mean, 3),
    " (", nrow(ocean_loc_summary_valid), " of ", nrow(ocean_loc_summary), " locations had a valid fit)\n", sep = ""
  )
} else {
  cat("Ocean location slope heterogeneity test could not be run: fewer than 2 locations had a valid C-PSD fit.\n")
}

Particle volume

Note: ocean’s fragment volume fit uses the same length/width-consistent volume_lod_bounds() approach as river and sediment (Section 4.2.3). Its fiber fit does not: ocean has only 480 fiber particles total, and even the corrected (length/width-consistent, not isotropic) fiber volume-LOD window contains just 4 of them — too few to constrain a fit. Ocean’s fiber volume fit instead falls back to the Segur algorithm’s own auto-detected LOD window. Similarly, the “all” (pooled shapes) fit uses the fragment-only volume-LOD window rather than the fragment/fiber union: with only 480 fibers, the union window is dominated by a handful of sparse, noisy fiber-derived bounds and destabilizes the pooled fit (fragments outnumber fibers roughly 10:1 in this matrix, so anchoring “all” to fragment’s reliable range is the more defensible choice here).

Show the code 
r_med_frag_ocean  <- ratio_tbl_ocean$r_med[ratio_tbl_ocean$shape == "fragment"]
r_med_fiber_ocean <- ratio_tbl_ocean$r_med[ratio_tbl_ocean$shape == "fiber"]
vlb_ocean <- volume_lod_bounds(cpsd_fit_ocean_frag, cpsd_fit_ocean_fiber, r_med_frag_ocean, r_med_fiber_ocean)
cat("Ocean fragment volume LOD: [", signif(vlb_ocean$fragment[1], 2), ",", signif(vlb_ocean$fragment[2], 2), "] µm³\n")
Ocean fragment volume LOD: [ 65000 , 8200000 ] µm³
Show the code 
cat("Ocean fiber    volume LOD (informational only — too few particles to use as a fit constraint): [",
    signif(vlb_ocean$fiber[1], 2), ",", signif(vlb_ocean$fiber[2], 2), "] µm³\n")
Ocean fiber    volume LOD (informational only — too few particles to use as a fit constraint): [ 55000 , 6900000 ] µm³
Show the code 
# fragment and all use the same uniform vol_bin_um as river/sediment. fiber is the one
# documented exception (see note above): with only 4 particles inside its physically-
# derived window, no fixed window is viable, so it falls back to auto-detection
# (fit_range_um = NA) with a coarser bin width appropriate to its much wider absolute
# volume range (up to ~3e7 µm³, vs ~7e5 µm³ for fragment) — fine bins there would be
# almost entirely empty regardless of methodology, per the small-sample diagnosis above.
ocean_fiber_vol_bin_um <- 1e6
cpsd_fits_ocean_volume <- fit_cpsd_by_shape(
  raw_particles_ocean, value_col = "V_um3",
  config = list(
    fragment = list(bin_um = vol_bin_um,          fit_range_um = vlb_ocean$fragment),
    fiber    = list(bin_um = ocean_fiber_vol_bin_um, fit_range_um = c(NA_real_, NA_real_)),
    all      = list(bin_um = vol_bin_um,          fit_range_um = vlb_ocean$fragment)
  )
)
cpsd_fit_volume_ocean_frag  <- cpsd_fits_ocean_volume$fragment
cpsd_fit_volume_ocean_fiber <- cpsd_fits_ocean_volume$fiber
cpsd_fit_volume_ocean       <- cpsd_fits_ocean_volume$all
Show the code 
# "all" uses the fragment volume window, as the C-PSD fit does (fibers are ~10% of ocean particles).
cpsd_fit_volume_ocean_cpsd <- cpsd_fit_volume_ocean
if (identical(slope_estimator, "tpl_mle")) {
  cpsd_fit_volume_ocean_frag  <- as_headline_fit(cpsd_fit_volume_ocean_frag, raw_particles_ocean$V_um3[raw_particles_ocean$shape == "fragment"], vlb_ocean$fragment)
  cpsd_fit_volume_ocean_fiber <- as_headline_fit(cpsd_fit_volume_ocean_fiber, raw_particles_ocean$V_um3[raw_particles_ocean$shape == "fiber"], vlb_ocean$fiber)
  cpsd_fit_volume_ocean       <- as_headline_fit(cpsd_fit_volume_ocean, raw_particles_ocean$V_um3, vlb_ocean$fragment)
}

12.0.1 River + ocean C-PSD fits (length, surface area, volume — faceted)

Combines the per-river-location fits (Section 4.2.4) with the pooled ocean fits above into one faceted comparison, now that both are available. Rows are shape, columns are size metric; y-axis (log10 cumulative count) is fixed across all panels so magnitudes are directly comparable, while the x-axis (log10 size) is left free per metric since length/area/volume span very different numeric ranges.

12.0.2 Slope comparison across matrices and metrics

Extends the per-river-location comparison (Section 4.2.5) with the pooled sediment (Section 11) and pooled ocean (Section 12.1) “all-shapes” fits for the same three size metrics, now that every matrix’s area and volume fits are available. Points are colored by matrix rather than location so the four within-river points read as one group against the single pooled sediment and ocean values; the reference line previously drawn at the Segur et al. (2026) literature fragment mean is omitted here, since that value is a single-shape (fragment), single-matrix (ocean-only) literature figure and is not a like-for-like reference for a plot that already includes this study’s own pooled matrix-level fits. The y-axis is fixed (not free) across the three metric facets so slope magnitudes are directly comparable panel to panel.

Show the code 
# Pooled ("all"-shape) sediment and ocean slopes, one row per metric, to sit
# alongside the four per-river-location rows already in loc_slopes_all
# (Section 4.2.5). Unlike river, sediment and ocean are not split by location
# here: sediment has no location field, and the ocean per-location fits
# (Section 12.0.1a) are length-only (area/volume were never fit per ocean
# location), so a single pooled point per matrix is the only like-for-like
# comparison available for all three metrics.
sed_ocean_slopes_all <- tibble::tribble(
  ~matrix,    ~metric,               ~a_cpsd,                    ~se_a_cpsd,
  "Sediment", "Length (µm)",         cpsd_fit_sed_all$a_cpsd,     cpsd_fit_sed_all$se_a_cpsd,
  "Sediment", "Surface Area (µm²)",  cpsd_fit_area_sed$a_cpsd,    cpsd_fit_area_sed$se_a_cpsd,
  "Sediment", "Volume (µm³)",        cpsd_fit_volume_sed$a_cpsd,  cpsd_fit_volume_sed$se_a_cpsd,
  "Ocean",    "Length (µm)",         cpsd_fit_ocean_all$a_cpsd,   cpsd_fit_ocean_all$se_a_cpsd,
  "Ocean",    "Surface Area (µm²)",  cpsd_fit_area_ocean$a_cpsd,  cpsd_fit_area_ocean$se_a_cpsd,
  "Ocean",    "Volume (µm³)",        cpsd_fit_volume_ocean$a_cpsd, cpsd_fit_volume_ocean$se_a_cpsd
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(group = matrix)

matrix_slopes_all_metrics <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  dplyr::mutate(loc_slopes_all, matrix = "River", group = as.character(location)),
  sed_ocean_slopes_all
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    metric = factor(metric, levels = c("Length (µm)", "Surface Area (µm²)", "Volume (µm³)")),
    group  = factor(group, levels = c(as.character(locations), "Sediment", "Ocean")),
    matrix = factor(matrix, levels = c("River", "Sediment", "Ocean"))
  )

matrix_pal_slopes <- c("River" = "#0072B2", "Sediment" = "#E69F00", "Ocean" = "#009E73")

cpsd_slopes_all_metrics_plot <- ggplot2::ggplot(matrix_slopes_all_metrics,
    ggplot2::aes(x = group, y = a_cpsd, color = matrix)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 4) +
  ggplot2::geom_errorbar(
    ggplot2::aes(ymin = a_cpsd - se_a_cpsd, ymax = a_cpsd + se_a_cpsd),
    width = 0.2, linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ metric, nrow = 1) +
  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = matrix_pal_slopes, name = "Matrix") +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x        = "Location (river) / matrix (sediment, ocean)",
    y        = expression(italic(a)[cpsd]),
    title    = "Headline slope (as a_cpsd = a_psd + 1) by location/matrix and size metric",
    subtitle = "Error bars = ±1 SE. River shown per location; sediment and ocean are pooled matrix-level fits."
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 20) +
  ggplot2::theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.border = ggplot2::element_rect(color = "gray85", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.4),
    strip.text   = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

12.1.1 All-matrix particle-length PSD comparison with MPSizeBase

This section is intentionally placed after the river, sediment, and ocean length C-PSDs have all been calculated. It imports the MPSizeBase workbook v19-5-2026 (Zenodo, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20832480, record v5, CC BY 4.0; file data_input/MPsizeBase v19-5-2026.xlsx, MD5 bd31cb5863cf1022f3717d219e2e6865, asserted below), reads the workbook Read Me, and parses one literature apsd value per PSD_ID from the Literature PSD data tab. The cumsum_powerlaw_alpha column is already the converted BN-PSD/differential slope (apsd = acpsd - 1), so no additional conversion is applied. This study’s rows show the headline slopes (maximum likelihood on a fixed 100–500 µm window). The MPsizeBase values are C-PSD fits, so the like-for-like comparison against our C-PSD fits is given in Section 13.6 (D4).

Results at a glance

River and ocean water (the quantitative headline result). At HC5, river water Food Dilution median RQ = 163.94 (P(RQ>1) = 98%) and Tissue Translocation median RQ = 0.177 (P(RQ>1) = 26.4%); ocean water Food Dilution median RQ = 8797.31 (P(RQ>1) = 100%) and Tissue Translocation median RQ = 0.765 (P(RQ>1) = 34.8%). A food-dilution threshold exceedance cannot be excluded, but it is method-conditional (floor-sensitive and driven by which toxicity studies enter the food-dilution SSD, not by exposure extrapolation alone – Section 12.5.1.3.1); Tissue Translocation is below threshold at the median for both matrices. The single-slope exposure correction (used above), a piecewise (dual-slope) bounding sensitivity, and an MLE/lognormal extrapolation-model comparison (Section 12.5.2) together bracket the sub-detection-limit extrapolation; all are quantified in the Sensitivity & structural uncertainty section below. Sediment is excluded from this conclusion: its exposure concentration is a per-liter water value with no dry-mass basis, not a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight measurement, and its nominal Food Dilution RQ (4,388,043, P = 100%) fails a benthic-plausibility guard by roughly eleven orders of magnitude (Section 11). A fully quantified executive summary, including the RQ decomposition that separates the exposure/length-slope/area-slope/volume-slope contributions, follows in Key Findings below.

Hoffman et al. (2026) frame the observed PSD as a transport-filtered distribution. A simple diagnostic is the capture fraction f(d, δ) = 1 − exp(−ws(d)·δ / K) and the critical size where ws(d)·δ / K ≈ 1. The calculation below uses Stokes settling/rise speed with user-supplied delta_m = 0.1 m and K_m2_s = 0.00001 m^2/s. These are assumptions, not measured site parameters, and should be replaced with field-specific values before a mechanistic transport correction is attempted.

Show the code 
matrix_fit_tbl <- tibble::tibble(
  Matrix = c("River water", "Sediment", "Ocean water"),
  cpsd_fit = list(cpsd_fit_all, cpsd_fit_sed_all, cpsd_fit_ocean_all),
  median_density_g_cm3 = c(
    median(raw_particles_river$density_g_cm3, na.rm = TRUE),
    median(raw_particles_sed$density_g_cm3, na.rm = TRUE),
    median(raw_particles_ocean$density_g_cm3, na.rm = TRUE)
  ),
  water_density_g_cm3 = c(1.00, 1.00, 1.025)
)

critical_piecewise_tbl <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(matrix_fit_tbl)), function(i) {
  fit_i <- matrix_fit_tbl$cpsd_fit[[i]]
  dc_i <- estimate_critical_size(
    delta_m = hoffman_delta_m,
    K_m2_s = hoffman_K_m2_s,
    density_g_cm3 = matrix_fit_tbl$median_density_g_cm3[i],
    water_density_g_cm3 = matrix_fit_tbl$water_density_g_cm3[i]
  )
  pw_i <- piecewise_cpsd_diagnostic(fit_i)
  tibble::tibble(
    Matrix = matrix_fit_tbl$Matrix[i],
    median_density_g_cm3 = matrix_fit_tbl$median_density_g_cm3[i],
    critical_size_um = dc_i,
    fit_lod_low_um = fit_i$lower_lod_used_um,
    fit_lod_high_um = fit_i$upper_lod_um,
    straddles_critical_size = is.finite(dc_i) && dc_i >= fit_i$lower_lod_used_um && dc_i <= fit_i$upper_lod_um,
    single_a_cpsd = fit_i$a_cpsd,
    single_a_psd = fit_i$a_psd,
    piecewise_break_um = pw_i$break_um,
    piecewise_low_a_cpsd = pw_i$slope_low,
    piecewise_high_a_cpsd = pw_i$slope_high,
    piecewise_delta_aic = pw_i$delta_aic
  )
}))

The piecewise fits are diagnostic only. A fit window that straddles the assumed critical size is flagged because the fitted single slope may blend a transport-distorted fine-size regime with the coarser-size regime. Per Hoffman et al. (2026), future refinement should prioritize measured 3-D geometry and polymer density over increasingly elaborate settling equations; even precise-geometry settling models retain substantial residual error, so settling-based corrections should be treated as bias-level adjustments rather than high-precision concentration estimates.

13.2.1 Single-slope vs. two-segment fits with binned data (particle length only)

Visualizes the two competing exposure-side models directly against the binned C-PSD data, using the same visual grammar as plot_cpsd_multi() (Section 4.2.1.1/Figure river_length_cpsd_plot): points outside the fitted LOD window shown at reduced opacity, dotted vertical lines marking the LOD window boundaries, and a 95% CI ribbon around each regression line. Restricted to particle length (the metric the piecewise bounding sensitivity, Section 13.3, actually uses); the analogous area/volume comparison is not produced, since the piecewise model is not fit for those metrics. Colors distinguish matrix (river/sediment/ocean); the two-segment panel’s break point for each matrix (Section 13.2 table above) is visible directly as the bend in that matrix’s line rather than marked separately, since the gap between the two fitted panels already makes the two-segment shape distinguishable from the single-slope one.

Show the code 
# Reuses the already-computed pooled "all"-shape length fits (no new fitting):
# cpsd_fit_all / cpsd_fit_sed_all / cpsd_fit_ocean_all for the single-slope
# model, and critical_piecewise_tbl$piecewise_break_um (this section, above)
# for where to split each matrix's two-segment model. The two-segment lines
# are obtained by refitting a plain lm(log10(N_ge) ~ log10(L_low)) separately
# on each side of the break, over the *same* LOD-window bins already selected
# by the single-slope fit (fo$data) -- i.e. an unconstrained-intercept version
# of the same segment-interaction model piecewise_cpsd_diagnostic() already
# fit to choose that break point, just refit here to recover per-segment
# intercepts for plotting (the diagnostic function only returns slopes/AIC).
cpsd_length_fits_by_matrix <- list(
  "River water" = cpsd_fit_all,
  "Sediment"    = cpsd_fit_sed_all,
  "Ocean water" = cpsd_fit_ocean_all
)
# Points/legend use the standard (medium-saturation) matrix palette; regression
# lines use a separately darkened variant of the same hues so the fit lines
# read clearly against the dense point cloud rather than blending into it.
matrix_pal_cpsd      <- c("River water" = "#0072B2", "Sediment" = "#E69F00", "Ocean water" = "#009E73")
matrix_pal_cpsd_dark <- c("River water" = "#00375C", "Sediment" = "#7A5300", "Ocean water" = "#00432F")

df_all_ms <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(cpsd_length_fits_by_matrix), function(mat) {
  fo <- cpsd_length_fits_by_matrix[[mat]]
  fo$bins |>
    dplyr::arrange(L_low) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      N_ge   = rev(cumsum(rev(n))),
      Matrix = mat,
      in_lod = L_low >= fo$lower_lod_used_um & L_high <= fo$upper_lod_um
    ) |>
    dplyr::filter(L_low > 0, N_ge > 0, n > 0)
}))

pred_single_ms <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(cpsd_length_fits_by_matrix), function(mat) {
  fo <- cpsd_length_fits_by_matrix[[mat]]   # headline fit (fixed-window MLE) -- drawn with fit_curve_logN()
  dplyr::mutate(fit_curve_logN(fo, seq(fo$lower_lod_used_um, fo$upper_lod_um, length.out = 200)), Matrix = mat, .before = 1)
}))

pred_piecewise_ms <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(cpsd_length_fits_by_matrix), function(mat) {
  fo  <- cpsd_length_fits_by_matrix[[mat]]
  brk <- critical_piecewise_tbl$piecewise_break_um[critical_piecewise_tbl$Matrix == mat]
  if (!is.finite(brk)) return(NULL)
  dat <- dplyr::mutate(fo$data, log_L = log10(L_low), log_N = log10(N_ge))
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(c("low", "high"), function(seg) {
    sub <- if (seg == "low") dplyr::filter(dat, L_low < brk) else dplyr::filter(dat, L_low >= brk)
    if (nrow(sub) < 2) return(NULL)
    fit_seg <- stats::lm(log_N ~ log_L, data = sub)
    grid    <- tibble::tibble(L_low = seq(min(sub$L_low), max(sub$L_low), length.out = 100))
    p       <- predict(fit_seg, newdata = data.frame(log_L = log10(grid$L_low)), se.fit = TRUE)
    tibble::tibble(Matrix = mat, segment = seg, L_low = grid$L_low, logN_fit = p$fit,
                   logN_lo = p$fit - 1.96 * p$se.fit, logN_hi = p$fit + 1.96 * p$se.fit)
  }))
}))

lod_bounds_ms <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(cpsd_length_fits_by_matrix), function(mat) {
  fo <- cpsd_length_fits_by_matrix[[mat]]
  tibble::tibble(Matrix = mat, xval = log10(c(fo$lower_lod_used_um, fo$upper_lod_um)))
}))

model_levels <- c("Single-slope (production)", "Two-segment (piecewise)")

df_both_ms <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  dplyr::mutate(df_all_ms, Model = model_levels[1]),
  dplyr::mutate(df_all_ms, Model = model_levels[2])
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(Model = factor(Model, levels = model_levels))

pred_single_ms    <- dplyr::mutate(pred_single_ms,    Model = factor(model_levels[1], levels = model_levels),
                                    line_color = unname(matrix_pal_cpsd_dark[Matrix]))
pred_piecewise_ms <- dplyr::mutate(pred_piecewise_ms, Model = factor(model_levels[2], levels = model_levels),
                                    line_color = unname(matrix_pal_cpsd_dark[Matrix]))

lod_bounds_both_ms <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  dplyr::mutate(lod_bounds_ms, Model = model_levels[1]),
  dplyr::mutate(lod_bounds_ms, Model = model_levels[2])
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(Model = factor(Model, levels = model_levels))

# Layer order matters: points are drawn first, then a dark "halo" line
# (thicker, neutral grey, semi-transparent) beneath the actual colored fit
# line, so the fit line reads clearly on top of the point cloud regardless of
# how dense the points are. The fit lines themselves use matrix_pal_cpsd_dark
# via aes(color = I(line_color)) -- a literal (AsIs) color that bypasses the
# shared discrete color scale, so lines can be darker than points without a
# second/conflicting legend.
cpsd_single_vs_piecewise_plot <- ggplot2::ggplot(df_both_ms, ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), y = log10(N_ge), color = Matrix)) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(
    data = lod_bounds_both_ms, ggplot2::aes(xintercept = xval),
    linetype = "dotted", color = "gray55", linewidth = 0.6, inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(alpha = in_lod), size = 1.3) +

    data = pred_single_ms, ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), ymin = logN_lo, ymax = logN_hi, fill = Matrix),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.15, color = NA
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_ribbon(
    data = pred_piecewise_ms,
    ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), ymin = logN_lo, ymax = logN_hi, fill = Matrix, group = interaction(Matrix, segment)),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.15, color = NA
  ) +
  # Dark halo behind the single-slope line (contrast against the point cloud).
  ggplot2::geom_line(
    data = pred_single_ms, ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), y = logN_fit, group = Matrix),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, color = "grey15", alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 2.6
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(
    data = pred_single_ms, ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), y = logN_fit, color = I(line_color), group = Matrix),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 1.4, alpha = 1
  ) +
  # Dark halo behind the piecewise lines.
  ggplot2::geom_line(
    data = pred_piecewise_ms,
    ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), y = logN_fit, group = interaction(Matrix, segment)),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, color = "grey15", alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 2.6

    subtitle = "Dotted = fitted LOD window boundaries. Faded points = outside LOD window. In the two-segment panel, the break is where each matrix's line visibly bends.",
    x        = expression(log[10] * "(Length, " * mu * "m)"),

13.3 Piecewise (dual-slope) PSD as a bounding exposure case

The production correction_factor() extrapolates a single fitted power-law slope from the measured LOD window down to the 1 um target floor. The two-segment diagnostic above (§13.2) shows the data themselves often prefer a shallower fine-size slope below a break point and a steeper coarse-size slope above it (river ΔAIC in the diagnostic table strongly favors the two-segment model; sediment likewise). Because the sub-floor extrapolation zone (1 um to the fitted LOD) can straddle or sit near that break — and because the fitted critical size d_c for river (~36 um) falls inside that 1-50 um extrapolation zone rather than inside the fit window itself — a single coarse slope may not be the right model to extrapolate through that zone. Independent evidence that single power laws mis-extrapolate to small, unmeasured sizes: in the St Louis Estuary, a single power law extrapolated to 1.3-12 particles/L for 5-5000 um while flow cytometry directly measured 600-1,600 particles/L in the same system (Thomas et al. 2024), and Segur et al. (2026) find size-aligned 1-5000 um concentrations average ~600x higher than reported values based on single-slope extrapolation. Both are cited as evidence that single-power-law extrapolation to small sizes is unreliable in general, not as a validated correction for this dataset.

correction_factor_piecewise() (R/mp_risk_utils.R, SPEC 2b) implements the two-segment alternative: it integrates dN/dL = kL^a using the fine-segment differential slope over [1, break_um] and the coarse-segment differential slope over [break_um, 5000], with the coarse segment’s density scaled so the two segments meet exactly (are continuous) at break_um. The piecewise cumulative slopes from the §13.2 diagnostic are converted to the differential convention (a_psd = a_cpsd - 1) internally via slope_convention = "cumulative", consistent with the SPEC 1c guard. This is a labeled bounding sensitivity, not a replacement for the single-slope production CF — the production exposure pipeline (Sections 5-6, 9-10, 12) is unchanged. The 1 um-LOD_low sub-window is unconstrained by data in both* the single-slope and piecewise case; the piecewise result quantifies structural (model-form) uncertainty in how that unconstrained sub-window is extrapolated, which is not captured by the Gaussian slope_structural_sd already added to the fit-uncertainty propagation.

Show the code 
piecewise_cf_row <- function(matrix_label, piecewise_row, L_meas_min, L_meas_max) {
  brk <- piecewise_row$piecewise_break_um
  s_lo <- piecewise_row$piecewise_low_a_cpsd
  s_hi <- piecewise_row$piecewise_high_a_cpsd
  if (!is.finite(brk) || !is.finite(s_lo) || !is.finite(s_hi)) {
    return(tibble::tibble(Matrix = matrix_label, break_um = NA_real_, cf_piecewise = NA_real_))
  }
  cf_pw <- correction_factor_piecewise(
    a_low = s_lo, a_high = s_hi, break_um = brk,
    L_meas_min = L_meas_min, L_meas_max = L_meas_max,
    L_tar_min = 1, L_tar_max = 5000,
    slope_convention = "cumulative"
  )
  tibble::tibble(Matrix = matrix_label, break_um = brk, cf_piecewise = cf_pw)
}

pw_river <- piecewise_cf_row("River water", dplyr::filter(critical_piecewise_tbl, Matrix == "River water"), L_meas_min_use, L_meas_max_use)
pw_sed   <- piecewise_cf_row("Sediment",    dplyr::filter(critical_piecewise_tbl, Matrix == "Sediment"),    L_meas_min_use_sed, L_meas_max_use_sed)
pw_ocean <- piecewise_cf_row("Ocean water", dplyr::filter(critical_piecewise_tbl, Matrix == "Ocean water"), L_meas_min_ocean, L_meas_max_ocean)

# Piecewise sensitivity is an exposure-only (CF/EED) effect: apply the single
# piecewise CF point estimate to the raw per-sample measured concentrations,
# then bootstrap the EED exactly as for the single-slope case. Hazard (haz*)
# is unchanged, so any RQ shift below is attributable to the piecewise CF alone.
set.seed(9401)
eed_boot_piecewise_river <- if (is.finite(pw_river$cf_piecewise)) {
  bootstrap_eed(monitoring_pooled_scope$C_measured_pL * pw_river$cf_piecewise, n_boot = n_boot, probs = c(0.5, 0.95))
} else NULL
set.seed(9402)
eed_boot_piecewise_sed <- if (is.finite(pw_sed$cf_piecewise)) {
  bootstrap_eed(monitoring_sed$C_measured_pkg * pw_sed$cf_piecewise, n_boot = n_boot, probs = c(0.5, 0.95))
} else NULL
set.seed(9403)
eed_boot_piecewise_ocean <- if (is.finite(pw_ocean$cf_piecewise)) {
  bootstrap_eed(monitoring_ocean$C_measured_pL * pw_ocean$cf_piecewise, n_boot = n_boot, probs = c(0.5, 0.95))
} else NULL

set.seed(9411)

  # Two-segment exposure vs the pooled single-slope hazard: the one documented

  draw_rq_mc1d(haz_pooled, eed_boot_piecewise_river$q50, n_risk = n_risk)

  dplyr::arrange(Matrix, ERM, Case)

# 95% CI (2.5th-97.5th percentile of the underlying 1D risk draws) for the
# plot's error bars -- summarize_rq() itself only returns p50/p95/p99, so the
# lower bound is computed here directly from each case's already-existing raw
# draws object (river/ocean single-slope: risk_draws/risk_draws_ocean, already
# built in Sections 8/12.4; piecewise: risk_draws_piecewise_river/_ocean,
# saved alongside their summaries above) rather than retrofitting summarize_rq().
rq_ci_from_draws <- function(draws, matrix_label, case_label) {
  if (is.null(draws)) return(NULL)
  draws |>
    dplyr::filter(ERM %in% c("Food Dilution", "Tissue Translocation"), HCx == 5) |>
    dplyr::group_by(ERM) |>
    dplyr::summarise(RQ_p025 = stats::quantile(RQ, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE),
                      RQ_p975 = stats::quantile(RQ, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    dplyr::mutate(Matrix = matrix_label, Case = case_label)
}

rq_bounding_ci <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  rq_ci_from_draws(risk_draws,                 "River water", "Single-slope (production)"),
  rq_ci_from_draws(risk_draws_piecewise_river,  "River water", "Piecewise (bounding)"),
  rq_ci_from_draws(risk_draws_ocean,            "Ocean water", "Single-slope (production)"),
  rq_ci_from_draws(risk_draws_piecewise_ocean,  "Ocean water", "Piecewise (bounding)")
)

rq_bounding_plot

Bounding range interpretation. The table above states, per matrix, the single-slope production RQ alongside the piecewise-sensitivity RQ; whichever is larger sets the upper bound of the sensitivity range and whichever is smaller sets the lower bound. Because the fine-size (sub-break) slope from the §13.2 diagnostic is shallower than the coarse-size slope for the matrices where the two-segment model is favored, the piecewise CF is expected to sit below the single-slope CF (less extrapolated mass assigned to the unconstrained 1 um-LOD_low zone) — i.e., the piecewise bound is expected to narrow the exposure (and therefore RQ) estimate relative to the single-slope production value, not widen it, for this dataset. This is stated as an expectation to be read against the rendered numbers above, not assumed; if a matrix’s piecewise CF instead exceeds the single-slope CF, that reversal is itself informative about how sensitive the conclusion is to the extrapolation model and should be flagged rather than averaged away. Regardless of direction, the single-slope CF remains the production default per the guardrails in the corrective-revision spec; the piecewise result is reported here strictly as a labeled sensitivity bound. Sediment caveat (SPEC 1d): the Sediment column/row above is illustrative only, for the same reason noted in Section 13.1/11.3.0 — its exposure concentration is not a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight value.

13.4 Benchmark against Dutch river datasets (RIVM 2026-0069)

This section compares this study’s particle-length PSD slopes and rescaled concentrations with water-based (per-volume) Dutch river data compiled for RIVM letter report 2026-0069 (Quik et al. 2026; data and code: rivm-syso/MicroplasticsERA_water, EUPL-1.2). The Dutch concentrations come from Mintenig et al. (2020; Meuse and Dommel, FTIR), Mughini-Gras et al. (2021; Rhine at Lobith and Lek canal at Vianen, LDIR) and Mintenig, Hunnestad & Koelmans (2025; Dommel, FTIR). The Dutch slopes are RIVM’s published poweRlaw maximum-likelihood fits (param == "longest"), and they are used as published: no Dutch particle data are refitted here. All logic is in R/rivm_utils.R. This child document only orchestrates it, and it is self-contained: it saves and restores the global RNG state, so it does not change any upstream or downstream result.

Windows. W2 = 50–500 µm is the primary comparison: it is this study’s sieve window and lies inside both Dutch measured ranges (20–5000 µm FTIR; 10–500 µm LDIR), so it needs interior rescaling only. W1 = 1–5000 µm is the Koelmans et al. (2020) default and a long extrapolation for every dataset. Measured window for this study. Following RIVM’s treatment of the Dutch data (rescaling from the sampling limits LLm/ULm), this study’s concentrations are rescaled from the 50/500 µm sampling sieves (rivm_L_meas_ours). This is a benchmark-only setting and does not change the pipeline’s L_meas_min_use/L_meas_max_use (Section 5.1). Slopes for this study. Each river’s own headline slope (maximum likelihood for a power law truncated at both ends of the fixed 100–500 µm window; Section 4.2.1.0) is used for both rescaled concentrations and slope comparisons, matching the pipeline default (slope_application). Like the Dutch slopes, these are maximum-likelihood fits to individual particle sizes.

Inputs and exclusions. Inputs were read from RIVM clone (rebuilt derived CSVs). In total, 37 Dutch surface-water samples were retained and 16 were excluded (table below): WWTP effluent; the nine Mintenig et al. (2020) samples analysed only above 300 µm, which have no total in Corrected_concentrations_total; and the four Mughini-Gras et al. (2021) samples without a reported total. Bäuerlein et al. (2022, 2023) particle data are not public. Their slopes appear in the slope comparison, but their samples are excluded from the concentration figures. For this study, the per-sample concentration is the sum over plastic polymer classes of the pipeline’s monitoring$C_measured_pL (56 samples, ×1000 to particles m⁻³).

Results. Rescaled to the common 50–500 µm window (W2), the Dutch water-body medians were 250 (IQR 160–310; n = 11) (Meuse, FTIR), 350 (IQR 98–1,600; n = 22) (Dommel, FTIR), 9,000 (range 5,500–13,000; n = 2) (Rhine, LDIR) and 3,200 (range 1,500–4,800; n = 2) (Lek canal, LDIR) particles m⁻³. W1 is secondary to the W2 comparison because it is a long extrapolation.

Caveats. (1) Slopes are method-dependent, so W1 differences conflate PSD shape with fitting method. (2) Dutch FTIR slopes were fitted above xmin ≈ 170–270 µm but are applied down to 20 µm. (3) LDIR and FTIR slopes differ systematically (α ≈ 2.4–3.8 versus 2.3–2.4). (4) Dutch concentrations are study-reported totals, not recomputed from particles. (5) This study’s samples are discrete pumped samples from small, episodic rivers; the Dutch samples come from large perennial rivers. (6) W2 is the primary comparison and W1 is secondary.

13.5 Anchor and shape sensitivities (spec/MPSizeBase.md Part B) and slope-SE realism (Part C)

These are supplementary sensitivities. None of them changes the production exposure: LOD-anchored, particle-rebuilt sample concentrations rescaled with each river’s own single slope. They answer three questions. How much does the exposure depend on where the concentration is anchored (S-A)? How much of the between-sample spread comes from the sample-specific in-window fraction (S-B)? What happens if fragments and fibers are rescaled with their own slopes rather than one pooled slope (S-C)? Every CF and concentration quoted in this section is labelled with its anchor, slope source and window (S-D). This child saves and restores the global RNG state, so it does not change any later result.

Show the code 
anchor_rng_state <- if (exists(".Random.seed", envir = globalenv())) get(".Random.seed", envir = globalenv()) else NULL
anchor_params <- list()
q_summ <- function(x) c(median = stats::median(x), q25 = stats::quantile(x, 0.25, names = FALSE),
                        q75 = stats::quantile(x, 0.75, names = FALSE))
# Share of the 1-5000 um count lying below 10 um for a differential slope a (< -1).
share_below_10 <- function(a) (1 - 10^(a + 1)) / (1 - 5000^(a + 1))

S-A. Dual anchor: LOD-anchored (production) vs sieve-anchored

Arm A is the production monitoring table: the concentration within the headline fit window (100–500 µm). Arm B anchors the same samples at the nominal 50–500 µm sieve window with the reported concentration. Both arms use the identical river-specific slope draws (alpha_by_river). The diagnostic compares the in-window fraction the river’s power law predicts, (L₂^(a+1) − L₁^(a+1)) / (500^(a+1) − 50^(a+1)), with the observed lod_particle_fraction.

Show the code 
anchor_B_mon <- monitoring |>
  dplyr::mutate(Lmin_measured_um = 50, Lmax_measured_um = 500, C_measured_pL = C_reported_pL)
anchor_run <- function(mon, seed) withr::with_seed(seed, correct_and_bootstrap_eed(
  monitoring = mon, conc_col = "C_measured_pL", cpsd_fit = cpsd_fit_all, alpha_draws = alpha,
  L_tar_min = 1, L_tar_max = 5000, n_draws = 3000, n_boot = n_boot, probs = c(0.5, 0.95),
  slope_convention = "differential", group_col = "river", cpsd_fit_by_group = cpsd_fits_by_loc,
  alpha_draws_by_group = alpha_by_river))
anchor_A <- anchor_run(monitoring, 13501)
anchor_B <- anchor_run(anchor_B_mon, 13501)

anchor_W1 <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  dplyr::mutate(anchor_A$C_sample_median, arm = "A_LOD"),
  dplyr::mutate(anchor_B$C_sample_median, arm = "B_sieve")) |>
  dplyr::left_join(dplyr::distinct(monitoring, sample_id, river, depth = sample_depth_general), by = "sample_id")
anchor_sa_tbl <- anchor_W1 |>
  dplyr::group_by(river, depth, arm) |>
  dplyr::summarise(W1_median = stats::median(C_corr_med), W1_q25 = stats::quantile(C_corr_med, 0.25),
                   W1_q75 = stats::quantile(C_corr_med, 0.75), .groups = "drop") |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = arm, values_from = c(W1_median, W1_q25, W1_q75)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(ratio_A_over_B = W1_median_A_LOD / W1_median_B_sieve)

anchor_frac_diag <- monitoring |>
  dplyr::mutate(a = vapply(river, function(r) cpsd_fits_by_loc[[r]]$a_psd, numeric(1)),
                predicted_fraction = (Lmax_measured_um^(a + 1) - Lmin_measured_um^(a + 1)) / (500^(a + 1) - 50^(a + 1)),
                low_n_flag = n_particles_lod_window < 10) |>
  dplyr::select(sample_id, river, depth = sample_depth_general, Lmin_measured_um, Lmax_measured_um,
                n_particles_lod_window, observed_fraction = lod_particle_fraction, predicted_fraction, low_n_flag)

S-B. Variance-reduced anchor

The sample-specific in-window fraction is noisy when a sample has few particles in the window. S-B replaces it with each river’s pooled fraction (Σ in-window particles ÷ Σ in-range particles), applied to the sample-specific reported concentration, and reports the effect on EED spread and on the number of zero-concentration samples.

Show the code 
anchor_pooled_frac <- monitoring |>
  dplyr::group_by(river) |>
  dplyr::summarise(pooled_fraction = sum(n_particles_lod_window) / sum(n_particles_reported_window), .groups = "drop")
anchor_SB_mon <- monitoring |>
  dplyr::left_join(anchor_pooled_frac, by = "river") |>
  dplyr::mutate(C_measured_pL = C_reported_pL * pooled_fraction)
anchor_SB <- anchor_run(anchor_SB_mon, 13501)

  arm = c("Production (sample-specific, particle-rebuilt)", "S-B (river pooled fraction x reported)"),
  n_zero_samples = c(sum(monitoring$C_measured_pL == 0), sum(anchor_SB_mon$C_measured_pL == 0)),
  W1_median = c(stats::median(anchor_A$C_sample_median$C_corr_med), stats::median(anchor_SB$C_sample_median$C_corr_med)),
  EED_q50 = c(stats::median(anchor_A$eed_boot$q50), stats::median(anchor_SB$eed_boot$q50)),
  EED_q95 = c(stats::median(anchor_A$eed_boot$q95), stats::median(anchor_SB$eed_boot$q95)),

S-C. Shape-stratified rescaling (sensitivity bracket, not a competing estimate)

Each shape’s in-window concentration is that shape’s QC-passing particle count inside the shape’s own LOD window, times the sample’s per-particle concentration (C_reported_pL / count). So the shapes sum to an all-shape total on the same basis as production. Shape slopes come from the pooled river fragment and fiber fits (headline fixed-window MLE, both on the same length window). Per-river × shape fits are reported for validity only. Slopes are drawn independently per shape with slope_structural_sd, and also in a fully correlated case (shared quantiles). Shapes are summed per sample before bootstrap_eed(). Following Segur et al. (2026), the power law is assumed to hold down to 1 µm; they note that log-normal behaviour below ~20 µm may need revisiting as better 1–20 µm data become available.

Show the code 
shape_fits <- list(fragment = cpsd_fit_frag, fiber = cpsd_fit_fiber)   # headline fixed-window MLE fits
shape_valid <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(cpsd_loc_shape_length), function(r) dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(c("fragment", "fiber"), function(sh) {
  f <- cpsd_loc_shape_length[[r]][[sh]]
  tibble::tibble(river = r, shape = sh, valid = isTRUE(f$valid),
                 n_bins = if (isTRUE(f$valid)) f$n_bins else NA_integer_, r2 = if (isTRUE(f$valid)) f$r2 else NA_real_,
                 passes_rule = isTRUE(f$valid) && f$n_bins >= 3 && f$r2 >= 0.90)
}))))

shape_counts <- raw_particles_river |>
  dplyr::filter(Client_ID_MSSupdate %in% monitoring$sample_id) |>
  dplyr::mutate(in_win = (shape == "fragment" & length_um >= shape_fits$fragment$lower_lod_um & length_um < shape_fits$fragment$upper_lod_um) |
                         (shape == "fiber" & length_um >= shape_fits$fiber$lower_lod_um & length_um < shape_fits$fiber$upper_lod_um)) |>
  dplyr::count(sample_id = Client_ID_MSSupdate, shape, wt = in_win, name = "n_shape_lod") |>
  tidyr::complete(sample_id = monitoring$sample_id, shape = c("fragment", "fiber"), fill = list(n_shape_lod = 0L))
shape_mon <- shape_counts |>
  dplyr::left_join(dplyr::select(monitoring, sample_id, river, C_reported_pL, count), by = "sample_id") |>
  dplyr::mutate(C_shape_lod = n_shape_lod * C_reported_pL / count)

shape_alpha_indep <- lapply(setNames(names(shape_fits), names(shape_fits)), function(sh) withr::with_seed(
  13600 + match(sh, names(shape_fits)), alpha_dist(shape_fits[[sh]]$a_psd, shape_fits[[sh]]$se_a_psd, n = n_mc, structural_sd = slope_structural_sd)))
shape_u <- withr::with_seed(13610, stats::runif(n_mc))
shape_alpha_corr <- lapply(shape_fits, function(f) {
  sd_tot <- sqrt(f$se_a_psd^2 + slope_structural_sd^2)
  truncnorm::qtruncnorm(shape_u, a = -6, b = -1.1, mean = f$a_psd, sd = sd_tot)
})
shape_cf <- function(draws) lapply(setNames(names(shape_fits), names(shape_fits)), function(sh)
  correction_factor(draws[[sh]], shape_fits[[sh]]$lower_lod_um, shape_fits[[sh]]$upper_lod_um, 1, 5000, slope_convention = "differential"))
shape_arm <- function(draws, seed) {
  cf <- shape_cf(draws)
  idx <- withr::with_seed(seed, sample.int(n_mc, 3000, replace = TRUE))
  per_sample <- shape_mon |>
    dplyr::group_by(sample_id) |>
    dplyr::summarise(C_corr_med = stats::median(
      C_shape_lod[shape == "fragment"] * cf$fragment[idx] + C_shape_lod[shape == "fiber"] * cf$fiber[idx]), .groups = "drop")
  list(cf = cf, C_sample_median = per_sample,
       eed = withr::with_seed(seed + 1, bootstrap_eed(per_sample$C_corr_med, n_boot = n_boot, probs = c(0.5, 0.95))))
}
shape_indep <- shape_arm(shape_alpha_indep, 13620)
shape_corr  <- shape_arm(shape_alpha_corr, 13620)

anchor_sc_tbl <- tibble::tibble(
  arm = c("Production (river slopes, all shapes)", "S-C shape slopes, independent", "S-C shape slopes, correlated"),
  EED_q50 = c(stats::median(eed_boot$q50), stats::median(shape_indep$eed$q50), stats::median(shape_corr$eed$q50)),
  EED_q95 = c(stats::median(eed_boot$q95), stats::median(shape_indep$eed$q95), stats::median(shape_corr$eed$q95)),
  W1_median = c(stats::median(C_sample_median$C_corr_med), stats::median(shape_indep$C_sample_median$C_corr_med),
                stats::median(shape_corr$C_sample_median$C_corr_med)))
anchor_sc_cf <- tibble::tibble(

  CF_median = vapply(shape_indep$cf, stats::median, numeric(1)),
  share_below_10um = share_below_10(vapply(shape_fits, `[[`, numeric(1), "a_psd")))
anchor_sc_cf <- dplyr::bind_rows(anchor_sc_cf, tibble::tibble(

The fragment slope is much steeper than the fiber slope, so the fragment CF dominates the shape-stratified total, and almost all of that total lies below 10 µm. That is why S-C is a bracket and not a competing estimate: agreement or disagreement at 1–5000 µm is driven by the sub-10 µm extrapolation, not by measured particles.

Part C. Slope-SE realism: particle-level bootstrap per river

The headline slope SEs come from the observed Fisher information of the truncated power-law likelihood. As a check, each river’s particles are resampled and the fixed-window MLE is refit (1000 replicates; 1,000 at the production budget). Cochran’s Q and I² are recomputed with the bootstrap SEs.

Show the code 
slope_boot_reps <- if (is_production_budget) 1000 else 100
slope_boot <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(cpsd_fits_by_loc), function(r) {
  x <- raw_particles_river$length_um[raw_particles_river$sample_location == r]
  a <- withr::with_seed(13700 + match(r, names(cpsd_fits_by_loc)), vapply(seq_len(slope_boot_reps), function(i) {
    tryCatch(tpl_mle(sample(x, replace = TRUE), cpsd_fits_by_loc[[r]]$lower_lod_um, cpsd_fits_by_loc[[r]]$upper_lod_um)[["a_psd"]] + 1, error = function(e) NA_real_)
  }, numeric(1)))
  tibble::tibble(river = r, a_cpsd = cpsd_fits_by_loc[[r]]$a_cpsd, se_info = cpsd_fits_by_loc[[r]]$se_a_cpsd,
                 se_boot = stats::sd(a, na.rm = TRUE), boot_ci_lo = stats::quantile(a, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE),
                 boot_ci_hi = stats::quantile(a, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE), n_failed = sum(is.na(a)), reps = slope_boot_reps)
}))
Show the code

13.6 Ocean-water comparison with MPsizeBase (spec/MPSizeBase.md Part D)

MPsizeBase (Segur et al. 2026; Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20832480, record v5, CC BY 4.0) has no river, freshwater, sediment or beach rows, and no California rows. Its ocean data come mostly from coastal Korea, the Mediterranean, the Atlantic and the Arctic. It is therefore an ocean-water and method comparator, not a validation; river water keeps the RIVM and Kooi benchmarks. The primary like-for-like comparison is the concentration inside the fully detected 165–385 µm window (Tier 2). Slopes (Tier 1) are compared shape-to-shape on the apsd convention, with each side’s fit window stated. Values rescaled to 1–5000 µm (Tier 3) are secondary, because almost all of that range lies below 10 µm and is extrapolated. The PSD counts also differ between the paper (81 binned fragment and fiber PSDs from 44 studies) and the v19-5-2026 sheet, which has more PSDs. This child saves and restores the global RNG state.

Show the code 
mpsb_rng_state <- if (exists(".Random.seed", envir = globalenv())) get(".Random.seed", envir = globalenv()) else NULL
mpsb_params <- list()
mpsb_file <- file.path(proj_root, "data_input", "MPsizeBase v19-5-2026.xlsx")
# D0: integrity (Zenodo file list: MD5 bd31cb5863cf1022f3717d219e2e6865, 3.2 MB)
stopifnot("MPsizeBase MD5 mismatch" = unname(tools::md5sum(mpsb_file)) == "bd31cb5863cf1022f3717d219e2e6865")
mpsb_raw <- suppressWarnings(readxl::read_excel(mpsb_file, sheet = "Literature PSD data", skip = 2, .name_repair = "unique_quiet"))
W_lo <- 165; W_hi <- 385
mpsb_num <- c("Low_size", "High_size", "Bin_concentration", "filtered_low_size", "filtered_high_size", "cumsum_slope",
              "cumsum_log_intercept", "cumsum_powerlaw_alpha", "cumsum_MP_1_5000_mean", "PSD_MP_count",
              "reported_min_size", "reported_max_size")
mpsb_ocean <- mpsb_raw |>
  dplyr::filter(Sample_type == "Ocean") |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::all_of(mpsb_num), ~ suppressWarnings(as.numeric(.x))))
stopifnot("MPsizeBase ocean rows must all be MP/m3" = all(mpsb_ocean$Bin_concentration_units == "MP/m3"))
overlap <- function(lo, hi) pmax(0, pmin(hi, W_hi) - pmax(lo, W_lo))

mpsb_psd <- mpsb_ocean |>
  dplyr::group_by(PSD_ID) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    Study = dplyr::first(Study), Year = dplyr::first(Year),
    shape = dplyr::if_else(grepl("fiber", dplyr::first(MP_shape), ignore.case = TRUE), "fiber", "fragment"),
    detection = dplyr::first(Broad_detection_method), depth_class = dplyr::first(Sub_type1),
    location_class = dplyr::first(Sub_type2), sampling = dplyr::first(Broad_sampling_method),
    sample_name = dplyr::first(Sample_name), n_mp = dplyr::first(PSD_MP_count),
    bins_lo = min(Low_size), bins_hi = max(High_size),
    lod_lo = suppressWarnings(min(filtered_low_size, na.rm = TRUE)), lod_hi = suppressWarnings(max(filtered_high_size, na.rm = TRUE)),
    window_coverage = sum(overlap(Low_size, High_size)) / (W_hi - W_lo),
    direct_165_385 = sum(Bin_concentration * overlap(Low_size, High_size) / (High_size - Low_size), na.rm = TRUE),
    lod_window_conc = sum(Bin_concentration[!is.na(filtered_low_size)], na.rm = TRUE),
    reported_range_conc = sum(Bin_concentration, na.rm = TRUE),
    rep_lo = dplyr::first(reported_min_size), rep_hi = dplyr::first(reported_max_size),
    a_cpsd = dplyr::first(cumsum_slope), a_psd = dplyr::first(cumsum_powerlaw_alpha),
    b = dplyr::first(cumsum_log_intercept), ext_1_5000 = dplyr::first(cumsum_MP_1_5000_mean),
    .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::mutate(study_id = sub("_.*$", "", PSD_ID))

D1. Reproduce the prepared windows tables

The windows tables are regenerated with tools/mpsizebase_ocean_windows_v1.py from the checksum-verified workbook (run with the reticulate Python). The script defines an observed window (direct_165_385) as the reported bin concentrations overlapping 165–385 µm, with partial bins prorated linearly, valid only when the PSD’s reported size range covers the window. Its sample key is study × location × coordinates × date × depth × sample name × sampling × mesh × volume; PSD_ID letters are site codes, not shapes. A sample-level direct sum is kept only if every shape’s PSD covers the window. The spec’s acceptance numbers are asserted below.

All D1 acceptance numbers are reproduced and asserted: 99 ocean PSDs (90 FTIR, 7 Raman, 2 microscopy); 57 PSDs from 11 studies with an observed 165–385 µm window; 26 PSDs whose fitted LOD covers the window (fragments median apsd −2.94, n = 18; fibers −1.34, n = 8); and 40 samples with an observed sample-level sum, median 61.9 MP m⁻³ (25 coastal, 15 offshore; 20 pump, 10 CTD, 8 IS pump, 2 tow). cumsum_powerlaw_alpha = cumsum_slope − 1 holds exactly, and the 1–5000 µm column equals 10^b(1 − 5000^a′).

D4. Tier 1: slopes by shape

Show the code 
# MPsizeBase slopes are C-PSD fits, so the like-for-like comparison uses this
# study's C-PSD fits; the headline fixed-window MLE slopes are shown alongside.
our_ocean_slopes <- tibble::tibble(
  shape = c("all", "fragment", "fiber"),
  fit = list(cpsd_fit_ocean_all_cpsd, cpsd_fit_ocean_frag_cpsd, cpsd_fit_ocean_fiber_cpsd)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(a_psd = vapply(fit, `[[`, numeric(1), "a_psd"), se = vapply(fit, `[[`, numeric(1), "se_a_psd"),
                window = vapply(fit, function(f) sprintf("%.0f–%.0f µm", f$lower_lod_um, f$upper_lod_um), character(1))) |>
  dplyr::select(-fit) |>
  dplyr::mutate(a_psd_mle = c(cpsd_fit_ocean_all$a_psd, cpsd_fit_ocean_frag$a_psd, cpsd_fit_ocean_fiber$a_psd),
                se_mle = c(cpsd_fit_ocean_all$se_a_psd, cpsd_fit_ocean_frag$se_a_psd, cpsd_fit_ocean_fiber$se_a_psd))
boot_ci <- function(x, seed) { if (length(x) < 3) return(c(NA, NA))
  b <- withr::with_seed(seed, replicate(2000, stats::median(sample(x, replace = TRUE)))); stats::quantile(b, c(.025, .975), names = FALSE) }
mpsb_slope_tbl <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(c("fragment", "fiber"), function(sh) {
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(c("PSD level: all included", "PSD level: LOD covers 165-385", "Study level (mean per study)"), function(lv) {
    x <- switch(lv,
      "PSD level: all included" = mpsb_inclusion$a_psd[mpsb_inclusion$included_slope & mpsb_inclusion$shape == sh],
      "PSD level: LOD covers 165-385" = mpsb_inclusion$a_psd[mpsb_inclusion$included_slope & mpsb_inclusion$lod_covers_window & mpsb_inclusion$shape == sh],
      "Study level (mean per study)" = mpsb_study$a_psd_mean[mpsb_study$shape == sh])
    ci <- boot_ci(x, 13800 + nchar(lv))
    tibble::tibble(shape = sh, level = lv, n = length(x), median = stats::median(x),
                   q25 = stats::quantile(x, .25, names = FALSE), q75 = stats::quantile(x, .75, names = FALSE),
                   boot_ci_lo = ci[1], boot_ci_hi = ci[2],
                   ours = our_ocean_slopes$a_psd[our_ocean_slopes$shape == sh],
                   ours_window = our_ocean_slopes$window[our_ocean_slopes$shape == sh],
                   ours_headline_mle = our_ocean_slopes$a_psd_mle[our_ocean_slopes$shape == sh],
                   mann_whitney_p_descriptive = if (length(x) >= 3) stats::wilcox.test(x, mu = our_ocean_slopes$a_psd[our_ocean_slopes$shape == sh], exact = FALSE)$p.value else NA_real_)
  }))
}))

D5. Tier 2: concentrations in the fully detected 165–385 µm window (primary comparison)

This study’s ocean concentrations in 165–385 µm come straight from the particle rows with exact edges: the number of QC-passing particle rows in [165, 385) µm × the sample’s per-particle concentration (C_reported_pL / count) × 1000 L m⁻³. Only ocean samples with particle-level data are included. Our ocean samples have no recorded depth, so they are compared against both MPsizeBase depth classes.

Show the code

  dplyr::filter(Client_ID_MSSupdate %in% monitoring_ocean$sample_id) |>
  dplyr::count(sample_id = Client_ID_MSSupdate, wt = length_um >= W_lo & length_um < W_hi, name = "n_165_385") |>
  dplyr::right_join(dplyr::select(monitoring_ocean, sample_id, C_reported_pL, count), by = "sample_id") |>
  dplyr::mutate(n_165_385 = dplyr::coalesce(n_165_385, 0L), conc_m3 = n_165_385 * C_reported_pL / count * 1000)

  dplyr::transmute(mpsb_samples, source = "MPsizeBase", group = paste("all", depth_class), conc_m3 = direct_165_385))

D6. Tier 3: measured and rescaled concentrations by anchor

Figure 3 puts every comparison on one log axis as boxplots with all points. MPsizeBase values are sample totals (fragment + fiber PSDs of the same sample summed; the script’s sample key). The panels run from the most to the least like-for-like:

  1. Measured, identical window 165–385 µm: observed bins (MPsizeBase) vs QC-passing particle rows (this study), no extrapolation.
  2. Measured, identical window 50–500 µm: MPsizeBase observed bins vs this study’s reported 50–500 µm concentration (all 15 samples) and the particle-rebuilt value (6 samples with particle data).
  3. Measured, each study’s own reported range: unscaled reported concentrations.
  4. Rescaled to 1–5000 µm, LOD-anchored: observed fit-window concentration × CF from that window (production for this study).
  5. Rescaled to 1–5000 µm, reported-range anchored: reported concentration × CF from the reported range (for this study, the 50–500 µm sieve window with the ocean slope).
  6. Rescaled to 1–5000 µm, MPsizeBase published fit: 10^b(1 − 5000^a′), shown for reference.

Rescaled values are extrapolation-dominated: for this study’s ocean slope, 90.1% of the 1–5000 µm count lies below 10 µm. Summing fragment and fiber extrapolations per sample is our aggregation, not a quantity the paper reports.

Show the code 
share_below_10_d6 <- function(a) (1 - 10^(a + 1)) / (1 - 5000^(a + 1))
cf_safe <- function(a, lo, hi) ifelse(is.finite(lo) & is.finite(hi) & hi > lo & a < -1,
                                      suppressWarnings(((5000^(a + 1) - 1) / (a + 1)) / ((hi^(a + 1) - lo^(a + 1)) / (a + 1))), NA_real_)
# PSD level (all ocean PSDs), then summed to the script's sample key.
mpsb_key_cols <- c("Study", "Location", "Lat", "Lon", "Start", "Depth_inf", "Depth_sup", "Sample_name", "Sub_type1", "Sampling", "Mesh_um", "Volume_m3")
mpsb_t3 <- mpsb_psd |>
  dplyr::left_join(dplyr::select(mpsb_inclusion, PSD_ID, exclusion_reason), by = "PSD_ID") |>
  dplyr::mutate(b_lod_anchored = lod_window_conc * cf_safe(a_psd, lod_lo, lod_hi),
                c_reported_range = reported_range_conc * cf_safe(a_psd, rep_lo, rep_hi),
                share_below_10um = share_below_10_d6(a_psd)) |>
  dplyr::select(-dplyr::any_of(setdiff(mpsb_key_cols, "Study"))) |>
  dplyr::left_join(dplyr::select(mpsb_win, dplyr::all_of(c("PSD_ID", setdiff(mpsb_key_cols, "Study"))), Study_key = Study), by = "PSD_ID")
mpsb_t3$sample_key <- do.call(paste, c(lapply(mpsb_t3[, c("Study_key", setdiff(mpsb_key_cols, "Study"))], as.character), sep = "|"))
stopifnot("PSD -> sample key must reproduce the script's 79 samples" = dplyr::n_distinct(mpsb_t3$sample_key) == 79)
mpsb_sample_t3 <- mpsb_t3 |>
  dplyr::group_by(sample_key) |>
  dplyr::summarise(shapes = paste(sort(unique(shape)), collapse = "+"), lod_anchored = sum(b_lod_anchored),
                   reported_anchored = sum(c_reported_range), .groups = "drop")

src_levels <- c("This study: all 15 samples (reported)", "This study: 6 samples with particle data", "MPsizeBase: sample totals")

Why this study’s rescaled ocean values are higher than MPsizeBase

The gap at 1–5000 µm is methodological, not evidence that Monterey Bay coastal water is more contaminated. On identical measured windows this study falls inside the MPsizeBase range (panels 1–2). The chain below rebuilds the production value from the all-sample reported concentration, one step at a time (medians over samples).

Three causes account for the gap:

  1. Sample selection (step B, ×7.6). The particle-level export covers only the 2024 ocean samples, which are the high ones. The 9 samples without particle data (2025) have low reported concentrations: median 70 MP m⁻³, against 760 for the 6 samples with data. The particle-rebuild basis cannot use them, so the ocean exposure rests on the high-concentration samples only. An updated particle export is the most important single fix.
  2. Rebuild basis and blank correction (step C, ×1.7). QC-passing particle rows outnumber the summary counts, which appear to be blank-corrected; the rows are not. Field blanks hold a median of 11 QC-passing particles, about 55 MP m⁻³ for a 200 L sample. That is as much as an entire low-concentration sample. 90 of 99 MPsizeBase ocean PSDs are blank-corrected.
  3. Anchor and extrapolation (step D, ×1.3). The ocean fit window is 100–500 µm. It holds 60.9% of the 50–500 µm particles, against 44.4% predicted by the fitted power law (×1.4): the measured PSD is flatter than the fitted slope at the small end. Rescaling from the upper window then extrapolates most of the 1–5000 µm count below 10 µm (CF median 128).

Starting from the all-sample reported concentrations with the sieve anchor (step A), this study’s 1–5000 µm ocean value is comparable to MPsizeBase. The production ocean value is therefore an upper bound, conditional on the 2024 samples, the rebuild basis and the LOD anchor. It is not evidence of unusually high contamination.

Tier 4 (500–5000 µm, optional) is not run. The visually extracted large-particle fraction and the 11 MPsizeBase PSDs covering 500–5000 µm (mostly tows) are not comparable enough for a quantitative statement.

13.7 Power-law slope estimation: method robustness and a per-river comparison

The rescaled 1–5000 µm concentrations, and therefore the risk quotients, depend steeply on the fitted power-law slope. For the steepest rivers, more than 99% of the rescaled count comes from extrapolation below 10 µm. This section asks which slope estimator the literature considers most reliable, and compares the estimators on each river’s particle data. It also checks whether the steep slopes found for Pajaro and Salinas reflect the rivers or the estimator. Since 2026-10-15 the fixed-window MLE recommended here is the production (headline) estimator for all matrices (Section 4.2.1.0). This section documents why, and reruns the former C-PSD production as a sensitivity. This child saves and restores the global RNG state.

What the literature recommends

  • Least-squares regression on binned, log-transformed counts is biased. Fitting a straight line to a log-binned histogram gives biased exponents and unreliable uncertainties. Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) on the individual measurements is accurate and precise (White et al. 2008; Clauset et al. 2009). In simulation tests of eight size-spectrum methods, seven regression-based and one MLE, only MLE was consistently accurate and gave reliable confidence intervals. Regression variants also estimate different parameters, so their slopes are not directly comparable (Edwards et al. 2017).
  • When only binned data exist, the bin structure has to be modelled. Ignoring it biases the exponent even for fine bins; a likelihood that accounts for the bins removes the bias (Virkar & Clauset 2014; Edwards et al. 2020). Regressing the cumulative binned distribution is much less sensitive to bin width and comes close to MLE (Virkar & Clauset 2014).
  • The C-PSD method was built for binned literature data. Segur et al. (2026) adopt cumulative regression because most published microplastic PSDs are binned, and they validate it against MLE on three raw datasets. In those tests the C-PSD slope fell within one MLE standard deviation, deviating by +0.08 to +0.26. The reference method in that validation is MLE on raw particle sizes (Clauset et al. 2009, R package poweRlaw). That is also the method Kooi et al. (2021) used for their compartment-specific microplastic slopes, and RIVM used for the Dutch river slopes (Quik et al. 2026).
  • Undercounted large particles bias cumulative fits toward steeper slopes. Segur et al. (2026, “Upper size LOD”) note that the right-hand tail of a C-PSD slumps when large particles go uncounted. They state that such bins make the slope steeper and must be removed from the regression, and that the upper LOD depends on the sample volume and the fraction of the filter analysed. Removing those bins does not fully remove the bias, however: every cumulative point inside the window still counts the particles above it, so a deficit above the window bends the top of the fitted range downward.
  • Upper truncation needs an explicitly bounded model. The standard Clauset et al. (2009) procedure estimates only a lower bound (xmin) and can fail when the distribution is truncated at the top (Deluca & Corral 2013). For data inside a known window, the appropriate model is the doubly truncated power law (truncated Pareto). Its parameters have consistent maximum likelihood estimators (Aban et al. 2006), and Edwards et al. (2017) recommend MLE for this bounded power law.
  • The window must be set independently of the slope being estimated. The truncated MLE is unbiased only for a window chosen in advance. Reusing a window that an algorithm selected because the data look straight there (as the Segur positive-residual step does) introduces selection bias. The simulation below shows this directly.

Implication for this study. We have the individual particle measurements, so the literature’s reference method applies directly: MLE on unbinned data, bounded at both ends because the upper tail is incomplete. We set the window from detection considerations, not from the data. The lower bound is 100 µm, where µFTIR detection at 25 µm pixels becomes reliable (four pixels across; Section 10.2). The upper bound is 500 µm, the sieve boundary above which large particles are undercounted (below). The doubly truncated power-law MLE on 100–500 µm is the most defensible estimator for these data, and it is the headline estimator for river, ocean and sand. Length slopes use the 100–500 µm window; area and volume slopes, used for hazard alignment, use the windows implied by it. The C-PSD fits are kept for comparison with Segur et al. (2026) and MPsizeBase (Appendix B; SI Tables S7–S8). The table below shows where the two estimators diverge, and the sensitivity run shows what the divergence means for risk.

Per-river comparison of estimators

Show the code 
slope_rng_state <- if (exists(".Random.seed", envir = globalenv())) get(".Random.seed", envir = globalenv()) else NULL
slope_method_params <- list()
mle_window <- c(100, 500)   # detection-based fixed window (Section 10.2; 500 um sieve boundary)

# tpl_mle() (doubly truncated power-law MLE) is in R/mp_risk_utils.R.
# Bin-normalised (BN-PSD) regression inside the window, 5 um bins.
bn_psd_slope <- function(x, lo, hi, bw = 5) {
  b <- seq(floor(lo / bw) * bw, ceiling(hi / bw) * bw, by = bw)
  h <- graphics::hist(x[x >= min(b) & x < max(b)], breaks = b, plot = FALSE)
  d <- data.frame(m = sqrt(b[-length(b)] * b[-1]), y = h$counts / bw)
  unname(stats::coef(stats::lm(log10(y) ~ log10(m), d[d$y > 0, ]))[2])
}
Show the code 
blank_qc_len <- parts_all_ids |>
  dplyr::filter(sample_type == "field blank", !material_class %in% c("mineral", "organic matter"), !is.na(material_class))
blank_qc_len <- blank_qc_len[spectra_qc_pass(blank_qc_len), ]
n_field_blanks <- dplyr::n_distinct(blank_qc_len$Client_ID_MSSupdate)

slope_method_tbl <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(cpsd_fits_by_loc), function(rr) {
  sub <- raw_particles_river[raw_particles_river$sample_location == rr, ]
  x <- sub$length_um
  f <- cpsd_fits_by_loc_cpsd[[rr]]; lo <- f$lower_lod_um; hi <- f$upper_lod_um   # C-PSD fit and its Segur LOD window
  tf <- tpl_mle(x, mle_window[1], mle_window[2]); tw <- tpl_mle(x, lo, hi)
  stopifnot(abs(tf[["a_psd"]] - cpsd_fits_by_loc[[rr]]$a_psd) < 1e-8)   # equals the headline fit
  pl <- poweRlaw::conpl$new(x[x <= 5000]); est <- poweRlaw::estimate_xmin(pl); pl$setXmin(est)
  # Blank subtraction on the 5 um grid: remove the expected field-blank particles
  # (mean blank histogram x number of samples), then redo the C-PSD regression in the same window.
  br <- seq(0, ceiling(max(c(x, blank_qc_len$max_length_um)) / 5) * 5, 5)
  n_corr <- graphics::hist(x, br, plot = FALSE)$counts -
    dplyr::n_distinct(sub$Client_ID_MSSupdate) * graphics::hist(blank_qc_len$max_length_um, br, plot = FALSE)$counts / n_field_blanks
  N_ge <- rev(cumsum(rev(pmax(n_corr, 0))))
  dd <- data.frame(L = br[-length(br)], N = N_ge, n = n_corr)
  dd <- dd[dd$L >= lo & dd$L < hi & dd$n > 0 & dd$N > 0, ]
  blank_sub <- unname(stats::coef(stats::lm(log10(N) ~ log10(L), dd))[2]) - 1
  # Tail diagnostic: particles above the C-PSD window, observed vs expected from the fixed-window MLE slope.
  al <- -tf[["a_psd"]]; n_win <- sum(x >= lo & x < hi)
  exp_above <- n_win * (hi^(1 - al) - 5000^(1 - al)) / (lo^(1 - al) - hi^(1 - al))
  tibble::tibble(
    river = rr, n_particles = length(x), window_um = sprintf("%.0f–%.0f", lo, hi),
    cpsd_segur = f$a_psd,
    tpl_mle_fixed = tf[["a_psd"]], tpl_mle_fixed_se = tf[["se"]], tpl_mle_fixed_n = tf[["n"]],
    tpl_mle_segur_window = tw[["a_psd"]],
    bn_psd_window = bn_psd_slope(x, lo, hi),
    mle_xmin_poweRlaw = -pl$pars, mle_xmin_um = est$xmin,
    cpsd_blank_subtracted = blank_sub,
    above_window_observed = sum(x >= hi), above_window_expected = exp_above,
    tail_ratio = sum(x >= hi) / exp_above)
}))

slope_method_params$per_river <- slope_method_tbl

The table answers three questions.

  • Do estimators agree? For San Lorenzo, whose C-PSD window ends at 80–330 µm, the C-PSD and recommended MLE slopes differ by 0.09. For Carmel, Pajaro, Salinas, the C-PSD slope is 0.45 to 0.88 steeper than the truncated MLE on 100–500 µm.
  • Why do they disagree? Above each of those C-PSD windows, which end near the 500 µm sieve boundary, there are only 0.28–0.52 times as many particles as the 100–500 µm power law predicts. This is the right-tail slump described by Segur et al. (2026): the cumulative counts inside the window inherit the deficit, and the fitted slope steepens (see the observed-vs-fitted tail figure after the sensitivity table, figures/slope_tail_deficit.png). The xmin-only MLE (poweRlaw, the method behind the Kooi et al. 2021 and RIVM slopes) fits the same deficient tail above xmin and is steep for the same reason.
  • Is contamination the cause? No. Subtracting the expected field-blank particles from each river’s size bins moves the C-PSD slope by +0.06 to +0.30, a small shallowing. Blank particles are not smaller than river particles. Contamination inflates the concentrations (Section 4.2.2.1) but does not explain the steep slopes.

Simulation: estimator behaviour under incomplete detection

A synthetic check, so the comparison does not rest on our data alone. Particle lengths are drawn from a power law with a known differential slope (−2.4, close to San Lorenzo) between 50 and 5000 µm, 2,500 particles per replicate. Three scenarios: complete detection; large particles undercounted (above 500 µm kept with probability 0.4, as seen in three rivers); and small particles undercounted (detection rising linearly from 50% at 50 µm to complete at 100 µm). Each estimator is applied exactly as above.

Show the code 
sim_true <- -2.4
r_tpl <- function(n, a, lo, hi) { al <- -a; u <- stats::runif(n); (lo^(1 - al) + u * (hi^(1 - al) - lo^(1 - al)))^(1 / (1 - al)) }
sim_cases <- c("complete detection", "large particles undercounted", "small particles undercounted")
slope_sim <- withr::with_seed(13901, dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(sim_cases, function(case) {
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(if (is_production_budget) 100 else 30), function(i) {
    x <- r_tpl(2500, sim_true, 50, 5000)
    if (case == sim_cases[2]) x <- x[x < 500 | stats::runif(length(x)) < 0.4]
    if (case == sim_cases[3]) x <- x[x >= 100 | stats::runif(length(x)) < x / 100]
    f <- tryCatch(fit_cpsd_segur_r(x, bin_um = 5), error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(f)) return(NULL)
    pl <- poweRlaw::conpl$new(x); pl$setXmin(poweRlaw::estimate_xmin(pl))
    tibble::tibble(case = case, rep = i,
                   `C-PSD (Segur)` = f$a_psd,
                   `Truncated MLE, 100–500 µm` = tpl_mle(x, mle_window[1], mle_window[2])[["a_psd"]],
                   `Truncated MLE, Segur window` = tpl_mle(x, f$lower_lod_um, f$upper_lod_um)[["a_psd"]],
                   `MLE above xmin (poweRlaw)` = -pl$pars)
  }))
})))
slope_sim_tbl <- slope_sim |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-c(case, rep), names_to = "estimator", values_to = "a_psd") |>
  dplyr::group_by(case = factor(case, levels = sim_cases), estimator) |>
  dplyr::summarise(n_reps = dplyr::n(), mean_bias = mean(a_psd - sim_true), sd = stats::sd(a_psd),
                   rmse = sqrt(mean((a_psd - sim_true)^2)), .groups = "drop")

slope_method_params$simulation <- slope_sim_tbl
sim_bias <- function(case, est) slope_sim_tbl$mean_bias[slope_sim_tbl$case == case & slope_sim_tbl$estimator == est]

Results:

  • The fixed-window truncated MLE is close to the true slope in all three scenarios (bias +0.01, +0.00 and +0.00).
  • The C-PSD fit becomes too steep when large particles are undercounted (bias -0.40). The xmin-only MLE is also pulled steeper (-0.20).
  • The truncated MLE on the window chosen by the Segur algorithm is biased shallow even with complete detection (+0.45). That window is selected from the data, often at sparse large sizes. This is why the recommended estimator uses a window set in advance.

Sensitivity: exposure and risk with the former C-PSD slopes

Since 2026-10-15 the headline uses the fixed-window MLE slopes. Here the river assessment is rerun with the former production setup. Each river’s C-PSD slope is used with its own Segur LOD window, monitoring concentrations are re-scoped to those windows, and the C-PSD area and volume slopes are used for hazard alignment. Under the ALIGNMENT RULE, each river’s hazard is re-derived with the same C-PSD slope draws that rescale its exposure. The structural slope uncertainty (slope_structural_sd), concentration basis and Monte Carlo budget are unchanged.
