15.1 Revised uncertainty interpretation

The main unresolved methodological uncertainties are now: (1) µFTIR objective and the marginal 50–100 µm detection zone, (2) transport-induced PSD structural uncertainty described by Hoffman et al. (2026), and (3) the lower extrapolation floor and toxicity-study-inclusion rule quantified in Section 12.5.1.3.1. The Hoffman uncertainty can affect absolute concentrations through the CF exponent, and may also affect relative comparisons when surface/subsurface samples, fibers/fragments, or buoyant/settling polymers are mixed in a pooled single-power-law fit. The sensitivity analyses above therefore replace the older conclusion that no further correction was warranted. The calibrated interpretation is that a Food Dilution threshold exceedance cannot be excluded but is method-conditional (floor-sensitive and study-inclusion-driven, Section 12.5.1.3.1; further bracketed by the piecewise and MLE/lognormal extrapolation-model sensitivities, Sections 13.2 and 12.5.2) rather than an unconditional risk-dominance finding, while magnitude estimates should be read together with the slope-uncertainty, depth-stratified, density/buoyancy, and water-sediment coherence diagnostics.

15.2 Modeling priorities

Hoffman et al. (2026) indicates that 3-D particle geometry and density inputs should be improved before investing effort in more complex settling-velocity equations. The current report follows that guardrail by adding polymer-resolved density and buoyancy flags, making δ and K explicit assumptions in the critical-size calculation, and retaining settling-based diagnostics as bias-level sensitivity checks rather than high-precision corrections. Future transport work should prioritize measured particle thickness, density, and shape-specific behavior; settling-equation refinements alone should not be expected to remove the dominant uncertainty.

15.3 Revised executive summary

This section restates the executive summary with the corrected numbers now that every matrix’s corrected and legacy sensitivity pipeline (Sections 5-14) has been computed, per SPEC 3b.

(a) Corrected Food Dilution RQ, after SPEC 1b. At the production Monte Carlo budget (1000 parameter-matrix replicates, 20000 slope draws), the corrected median Food Dilution HC5 RQ is 117.073 for river water (P(RQ>1) = 95.9%) and 8797.306 for ocean water (median P(RQ>1) = 100%). Sediment is intentionally omitted from this headline figure (SPEC 1d): its nominal corrected Food Dilution HC5 RQ (4388042.962, P(RQ>1) = 100%) is not a defensible risk estimate — Section 11.3.0/11.4.0 trace this to a placeholder exposure concentration (a per-liter water value reused as particles/kg) and a derived HC5 that fails the benthic-plausibility guard by roughly eleven orders of magnitude — so it is excluded from the risk conclusion rather than reported alongside the river and ocean values.

(b) The prior (SPEC 1b-uncorrected) Food Dilution RQ was inflated by the volume-slope convention error. Reverting only a.v/a.sa/a.m to the legacy cumulative-as-differential convention (Appendix A), holding exposure and the length-slope alignment at their corrected values, the river-water Food Dilution HC5 median RQ becomes 14719501.481 — a 125729.3-fold change relative to the corrected value of 117.073. This is the same mechanism and direction of error described in the SPEC 1b background (a mean-particle-volume sensitivity calculation there estimates a ~4-6 million-fold effect at a = 0.76 vs. 1.68); the exact factor is a function of n_boot/n_mc and is expected to scale toward that estimate as the budget increases. No Food Dilution RQ figure in this report should be read as ~10^7 — that magnitude describes the pre-SPEC-1b (legacy) error being corrected here, not the corrected result.

(c) Tissue Translocation shift after both the length-slope and surface-area-slope fixes (revised, SPEC 3c). Reverting only the hazard-side length-slope alignment to its legacy cumulative-as-differential form, the river-water Tissue Translocation HC5 P(RQ>1) is 21.1%, versus 25.9% under the corrected alignment (Section 14.1). This is a material driver, but so is the surface-area slope: reverting a.v/a.sa/a.m together gives 67.7%, and isolating a.sa alone gives 66.5% — both far from the 25.9% corrected value, because Tissue Translocation/oxidative-stress alignment is surface-area-weighted and therefore directly sensitive to the a.sa correction, unlike its (correctly) minimal sensitivity to the volume slope alone. A prior version of this narrative incorrectly called the volume/area effect on Tissue Translocation “essentially unchanged”; that claim is retracted here (Section 14.1 has the corrected attribution and the full one-at-a-time decomposition table, now covering both ERMs).

(d) Exposure as a single-slope-vs-piecewise bounding range (SPEC 2b). The production single-slope correction factor and its piecewise (dual-slope) bounding alternative are compared per matrix in Section 13.3 (Tables: single-slope vs. piecewise CF/EED, and the resulting Food Dilution/Tissue Translocation HC5 RQ range). The single-slope CF remains the production default; the piecewise result is a labeled sensitivity bound quantifying structural (model-form) uncertainty in the unconstrained 1 µm-to-LOD sub-window, per the guardrails in the corrective-revision spec.

(e) Sediment pathway excluded from the headline conclusion (SPEC 1d). The sediment (beach sand) risk characterization in Section 11 is retained in this report as a methods/illustrative demonstration only. Its exposure concentration is not a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight value (Section 11.3.0), its hazard-side dose_unit = “kg” pathway was traced and found unit-consistent on its own terms with no discrete conversion bug identified (Section 11.4.0), and its sediment-specific ERM alignment slopes were independently verified correct and ruled out as the cause (Section 11.2, SPEC 1d-iv). The resulting sediment Food Dilution HC5 fails a rendered plausibility guard anchored on Redondo-Hasselerharm et al. (2023) by roughly eleven orders of magnitude. Until a genuine dry-weight sediment concentration is available, no sediment RQ in this report should be treated as a risk finding.

(f) Sediment as a time-dependent, accumulating compartment (SPEC 1e). Independent of the exposure-concentration problem in (e), Section 11.5 reframes sediment as an accumulating depositional sink in which deposited microplastics continue to fragment in place, so both bioaccessible exposure and hazard (HC5, via which benthic species become size-accessible) evolve over residence time (Thuy-Dung, Groenenberg & Koelmans 2026). Any static sediment metric — including the illustrative Section 11.4 figures — is therefore a lower-bound snapshot, not an equilibrium value. Section 11.5.2 demonstrates this illustratively with a labeled, non-quantitative PSD-shift sensitivity showing the derived Food Dilution and Tissue Translocation HC5 falling as the sediment PSD is shifted progressively finer; Section 11.5.4 adds a most-sensitive-species screen (sediment, plus a river/ocean companion) since individual-species risk can precede a derivable community SSD signal. This is a framework/sensitivity addition — it does not change point (e): sediment remains excluded from the headline risk conclusion.

Summary. A food-dilution threshold exceedance cannot be excluded but is not robust. At the field-standard 1 µm floor, the food-dilution RQ exceeds 1 in both matrices (river MC2D median RQ = 163.94, P(RQ>1) = 98%; ocean = 8797.31, P(RQ>1) = 100%), while Tissue Translocation is below threshold (river 0.177; ocean 0.765). This exceedance is conditional: it collapses (river Food Dilution RQ already much smaller by a 2.5 µm floor, 1.298) as the lower size floor rises from 1 µm (Section 12.5.1), and Section 12.5.1.3.1 shows it is generated by admitting <10 µm-tested toxicity studies into the volume-based food-dilution SSD (a hazard/HC5 effect) rather than by coherent sub-10 µm exposure extrapolation. With the study set held fixed and exposure and hazard rescaled coherently (Arm B, Section 12.5.1.3.1), the river food-dilution RQ at a 1 µm floor is 1.22 (1D) and 2.166 under MC2D, with ocean below 1 under both metrics (1D = 2199.646, MC2D = 2764.291). Because the ~1 particles/L food-dilution HC5 (production, tracking study set) reproduces the published field-standard value, this fragility is a property of the standard method, not of these sites – the fixed-study-set HC5 is ~6 by comparison. Tissue translocation is robustly below threshold across all floors (Section 12.5.1.3). Sub-10 µm exposure de-extrapolation is not negligible – it is the larger single lever by magnitude (river exposure-CF fold 24.85x vs composition fold 127.1x); read this as “study inclusion is decisive for threshold-crossing,” never as “extrapolation is irrelevant.” The exceedance’s magnitude is further bracketed by two exposure-model sensitivities: the two-segment (piecewise) fit (Section 13.2/13.3, river Food Dilution RQ 163.46) and the MLE/lognormal small-end extrapolation model (Section 12.5.2), both reported in the sensitivity sections above. The sediment pathway remains excluded from this conclusion pending real concentration data (point (e) above). The magnitude-uncertainty pointer here has shifted from the convention-fix audit to the floor / study-inclusion / extrapolation-model triad above; the three-convention-fix decomposition (point (b), Appendix A) remains in the report as an internal audit artifact, not as the principal driver of remaining magnitude uncertainty.

15.4 individual-species RCR — river/ocean companion screen

Section 11.5.4 added a most-sensitive-species screen for the sediment benthic dataset. This subsection completes SPEC 1e-iv’s companion request for the water compartments where exposure is quantitative (river, ocean): the single most sensitive species per ERM, plus the individual-species risk characterization ratio RCR = EED / lowest-species EC, reported as an early-warning companion to the community-HC5 RQ already characterized in Sections 7/12. This is placed here, after Section 15.3, because it is the first point in document execution order at which every matrix’s hazard (haz/haz_ocean) and EED (eed_boot/eed_boot_ocean) objects all exist together.

Show the code

mss_ocean <- most_sensitive_species(erm_registry_ocean, dose_col = "dose_new_particles_L")

  dplyr::mutate(mss_ocean, Matrix = "Ocean water",  .before = 1),
  dplyr::mutate(mss_sed,   Matrix = "Sediment",     .before = 1)
)

Per Thuy-Dung et al. (2026), an individual-species RCR>1 can precede a derivable community-HC5 RQ signal by roughly a decade — the table above is therefore read as an early-warning companion, not a substitute for the community-HC5 RQ already reported in Sections 7 and 12. This companion screen does not change any headline conclusion: it reuses the same production haz/eed_boot objects without modification, and is additive/diagnostic only.

Appendices

The three appendices below hold convention-validation history, implementation-validation detail, and exploratory/non-quantitative sediment material that support the results above but are not needed to read them. Every number in this document – including here – is produced by the same live code as the main body; nothing here is retyped. SPEC-numbered labels below are preserved from docs/CHANGELOG_hoffman_revisions.md, which is the authoritative provenance record for each revision.

Appendix A: Convention-validation history

The differential-slope convention (length, area, volume, mass; Sections 5, 7) is the current basis throughout this report. This appendix quantifies the effect of each prior convention error that the SPEC 1/1b/3b/3c revisions corrected, and is why no number in the report body should be read as the pre-fix (≈10⁷, Food Dilution) legacy magnitude.

A.1 all-matrix CF before/after (legacy cumulative vs. corrected differential)

Reruns the correction-factor convention check of Section 5.1 for all three matrices at once, comparing the legacy (cumulative slope passed as differential), corrected fit-only, and corrected structural-SD CF distributions side by side.

Show the code 
cf_case_summary <- function(matrix_label, cpsd_fit, combined_cf_current,
                            Lmin_use, Lmax_use, current_slope_draws, n = n_mc) {
  set.seed(4000 + nchar(matrix_label))
  cumulative_draws <- alpha_dist(mu = cpsd_fit$a_cpsd, sd = cpsd_fit$se_a_cpsd, n = n, structural_sd = 0)
  differential_fit_draws <- alpha_dist(mu = cpsd_fit$a_psd, sd = cpsd_fit$se_a_psd, n = n, structural_sd = 0)
  legacy_cf <- correction_factor(
    a = cumulative_draws,
    L_meas_min = Lmin_use,
    L_meas_max = Lmax_use,
    L_tar_min = 1,
    L_tar_max = 5000,
    slope_convention = "differential"
  )
  corrected_fit_cf <- correction_factor(
    a = differential_fit_draws,
    L_meas_min = Lmin_use,
    L_meas_max = Lmax_use,
    L_tar_min = 1,
    L_tar_max = 5000,
    slope_convention = "differential"
  )
  tibble::tibble(
    Matrix = matrix_label,
    Case = c("Legacy cumulative slope passed as differential", "Corrected differential slope, fit SE only", "Corrected differential slope plus structural SD"),
    Slope_p50 = c(median(cumulative_draws), median(differential_fit_draws), median(current_slope_draws)),
    CF_p05 = c(quantile(legacy_cf, 0.05), quantile(corrected_fit_cf, 0.05), quantile(combined_cf_current, 0.05)),
    CF_p50 = c(median(legacy_cf), median(corrected_fit_cf), median(combined_cf_current)),
    CF_p95 = c(quantile(legacy_cf, 0.95), quantile(corrected_fit_cf, 0.95), quantile(combined_cf_current, 0.95))
  )
}

cf_before_after_all <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  cf_case_summary("River water", cpsd_fit_all, combined_cf_pooled, L_meas_min_use, L_meas_max_use, alpha),
  cf_case_summary("Sediment", cpsd_fit_sed_all, combined_cf_sed, L_meas_min_use_sed, L_meas_max_use_sed, alpha_sed),
  cf_case_summary("Ocean water", cpsd_fit_ocean_all, combined_cf_ocean, L_meas_min_ocean, L_meas_max_ocean, alpha_ocean)
)

)

A.2 Food Dilution RQ decomposition (legacy cumulative vs. corrected differential a.v/a.sa)

The Section 13 table above (SPEC 1, from the prior revision) shows that the length-slope convention fix changes the exposure correction factor. The volume/area-slope fix in this revision (SPEC 1b) is a separate, hazard-side-only effect: it does not touch correction_factor() or the EED at all, only the particle-trait alignment used inside pSSD++ (a.v.*, a.sa.*, a.m.*). To make that effect auditable, this section re-runs the pSSD++ hazard alignment and 1D risk characterization for each matrix with a “legacy” parameter set in which only a.v/a.sa/a.m are reverted to the pre-fix cumulative-slope values (legacy_cumulative_av_params(), R/mp_risk_utils.R) — holding the length slope, R.ave, exposure (EED), and everything else fixed — so the entire before/after RQ change in this table is attributable to the volume/area-slope convention alone.

The volume/area-slope correction is confined to the hazard alignment: exposure concentrations, the EED, and combined_cf/combined_cf_sed/combined_cf_ocean are numerically identical between the legacy and corrected rows above (they are not recomputed in this section). The magnitude of the collapse in the Food Dilution HC5 median RQ therefore isolates the volume-slope error described in SPEC 1b, consistent with the mean-particle-volume sensitivity calculation in the spec (a.v = 0.76 vs. 1.68 implying an ~4-6 million-fold difference in mean particle volume, and a comparable inverse effect on the Food Dilution threshold and RQ). Correction (SPEC 3c): Tissue Translocation is not expected to be insensitive to this fix overall — it is insensitive to the volume slope specifically (its dose model is not volume-weighted), but it is materially sensitive to the surface-area slope reverted in the same combined row above, because Tissue Translocation/oxidative-stress alignment is surface-area-weighted; see Section 14.1 for the row that isolates a.sa alone and the corrected narrative. Sediment caveat (SPEC 1d): the Sediment rows above are illustrative/non-quantitative — their exposure concentration is not a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight value (Section 11.3.0) — so while they are retained here to confirm the volume/area-slope-convention mechanism holds across matrices, the absolute RQ magnitudes for Sediment must not be read as real risk estimates (Section 11.4.0, 15.3).

A.3 RQ decomposition — one-at-a-time convention reversions

Two convention fixes, made at different times, both change the Food Dilution risk quotient, for different reasons: (i) the exposure-side power-law correction factor (correction_factor(), Section 5.1) rescales the measured concentration; (ii) the hazard-side length-slope alignment (alpha.freshwater/alpha.marine/alpha.sediment.freshwater inside pSSD++, fixed in the prior revision) changes how toxicity endpoints are aligned to a common particle-size basis; and (iii) the hazard-side volume/area-slope alignment (a.v.*/a.sa.*/a.m.*, SPEC 1b, this revision) changes the polydisperse mean particle volume used by the Food Dilution dose model. This section isolates each of the three as a one-at-a-time sensitivity relative to the fully corrected river-water baseline, reverting exactly one piece to its legacy (pre-fix) form while holding the other two at their corrected values. River water is used as the representative matrix (the all-matrix table in Section 13.1 already shows (iii) holds for sediment and ocean water too).

Show the code 
# (i) Exposure correction factor reverted to legacy (cumulative-as-differential),
# hazard (haz) held at the fully corrected values. No pSSD rerun needed: this
# only recomputes the corrected-concentration draws with the legacy CF vector
# already computed above (A.1, legacy_cf_river).
set.seed(9202)
C_legacycf_draws <- monitoring_pooled_scope |>
  dplyr::mutate(idx = dplyr::row_number()) |>
  tidyr::crossing(draw = seq_len(3000)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    cf          = sample(legacy_cf_river, size = dplyr::n(), replace = TRUE),
    C_corrected = C_measured_pL * cf
  )
C_sample_median_legacycf <- C_legacycf_draws |>
  dplyr::group_by(sample_id) |>
  dplyr::summarise(C_corr_med = stats::median(C_corrected), .groups = "drop")
eed_boot_legacycf_river <- bootstrap_eed(C_sample_median_legacycf$C_corr_med, n_boot = n_boot, probs = c(0.5, 0.95))
set.seed(9307)
risk_summary_legacycf_river <- summarize_rq(draw_rq_mc1d(haz_pooled, eed_boot_legacycf_river$q50, n_risk = n_risk))
Show the code

# reverted together, length alpha and exposure corrected); (iv, SPEC 3c) isolates
# a.sa alone. Both ERMs (Food Dilution and Tissue Translocation) are reported,
# since SPEC 3c found the prior Food-Dilution-only table masked how the a.sa
# reversion affects the surface-area-weighted Tissue Translocation ERM.
rq_decomp_river_raw <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  dplyr::mutate(risk_summary_pooled,                 Contribution_reverted = "None (fully corrected, this revision)"),
  dplyr::mutate(risk_summary_legacycf_river,         Contribution_reverted = "(i) Exposure correction factor -> legacy cumulative-as-differential"),
  dplyr::mutate(risk_summary_legacy_alpha_river,      Contribution_reverted = "(ii) Hazard length-slope alignment -> legacy cumulative-as-differential"),
  dplyr::mutate(risk_summary_legacy_river,           Contribution_reverted = "(iii) Hazard volume+area+mass-slope alignment -> legacy cumulative (SPEC 1b)"),
  dplyr::mutate(risk_summary_legacy_asa_river,        Contribution_reverted = "(iv) Hazard surface-area-slope alignment ONLY -> legacy cumulative (SPEC 3c)")
) |>
  dplyr::filter(HCx == 5) |>
  dplyr::select(ERM, Contribution_reverted, RQ_p50, RQ_p95, P_exceed)

rq_decomp_corrected_baseline <- rq_decomp_river_raw |>

Reading the table: the ratio_vs_corrected column is how much larger (or smaller) each ERM’s HC5 median RQ becomes if only that one convention error were reintroduced, relative to that same ERM’s own fully-corrected baseline. Because this is a 1000-replicate development-scale run (production budgets are ≥1000 per the deliverables checklist), the exact ratios should be treated as directionally informative rather than final, and re-checked at full budget before external release.

SPEC 3c correction to the Tissue Translocation attribution. Tissue Translocation P(RQ>1) at HC5 moves from 21.1% under the legacy (cumulative-as-differential) length-slope alignment to 25.9% under the corrected alignment, confirming the length-slope fix (prior revision) is one material driver of the Tissue Translocation shift. However, the volume+area+mass reversion also moves Tissue Translocation P(RQ>1) materially, from 67.7% (legacy) to 25.9% (corrected) — a change of this size is not “essentially unchanged,” and a prior version of this narrative incorrectly claimed it was. Isolating the surface-area slope alone (a.sa reverted to legacy cumulative, a.v/a.m/alpha/exposure held corrected) reproduces most of that shift: P(RQ>1) is 66.5% under the legacy a.sa alone, versus 25.9% corrected. This is mechanistically expected: unlike Food Dilution (volume-weighted), Tissue Translocation/oxidative-stress alignment is surface-area-weighted, so it is directly sensitive to the a.sa correction (cumulative a.sa ≈ 1.3 → differential a.sa ≈ 2.3 for river water; Section 13.1/7.2) in the same way Food Dilution is sensitive to a.v. Tissue Translocation is not literally insensitive to SPEC 1b — it is insensitive to the volume slope specifically (because dose is not volume-weighted) but sensitive to the area slope (because dose is area-weighted). Corrected qualitative conclusion: after both the length-slope and area-slope fixes, river-water Tissue Translocation HC5 is below threshold at the median (RQ ≈ 0.177, P(RQ>1) ≈ 25.9%), while Food Dilution (RQ ≈ 124.601, P(RQ>1) ≈ 97.9%) remains risk-dominant.

Appendix B: C-PSD implementation validation

B.1 Segur PSD_fit.py run on W2W particle-length PSDs, compared with the native R implementation

Appendix C: Sediment (non-quantitative) and exploratory diagnostics

Sediment is excluded from the headline risk conclusion (Section 11) because its exposure concentration is not a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight value. The material below extends the sediment analysis for methods/illustrative purposes only – none of it should be combined with the Section 11 exposure figures to produce a sediment risk quotient.

C.1 sediment PSD-shift sensitivity (illustrative; production-gated)

This subsection implements sediment_psd_shift_sensitivity() (R/mp_risk_utils.R), which re-runs the full sediment hazard alignment (matrix_function() → run_pssd_pipeline() → build_haz_df()) across a grid of progressively finer sediment PSDs, representing continued in-situ fragmentation, and reports how the derived Food Dilution and Tissue Translocation HC5 respond as more particles fall below benthic bioaccessibility limits. A genuine hazard-side response (not merely a rescaled exposure number) requires this full re-run, because steepening the PSD changes the simulated particle-size population that pSSD++’s ingestible/translocatable size-gating operates on — i.e., it can change which species clear the bioaccessibility threshold and enter the SSD.

Gating. This sensitivity is gated on sediment_concentration_is_quantitative (currently FALSE, SPEC 1d-i). While FALSE it is run as an illustrative/methods demonstration only — every row below is explicitly labeled non-quantitative and excluded from the risk conclusion, analogous to the existing single-slope↔︎piecewise CF bound (SPEC 2b, Section 13.3). It becomes a production sensitivity feeding the sediment RQ range only once that flag is set TRUE.

What is not transplanted. Thuy-Dung et al.’s kfrag/shell-geometry fragmentation model is calibrated to polymer-coated-fertilizer prills with 7-year field data — a single, known-age, known-geometry polymer system — not the heterogeneous mixed-polymer sediment microplastics of unknown age sampled here. Rather than fit a kinetic rate that would not transfer to this dataset, the size-shift below is parameterized as an explicit, cited scenario grid: an added shift to the differential length/area/volume/mass slopes (alpha/a.v/a.sa/a.m.sediment.freshwater, positive-alpha convention — larger values are steeper/finer), applied identically across all four size metrics as a simplifying assumption (fragmentation is assumed to shift all size metrics proportionally).

Show the code 
# 0 = no shift (baseline -- an internal consistency check against
# Section 11.4's production sediment HC5, subject to Monte Carlo/parallel RNG
# noise since no fixed seed is threaded through PSSDplusplus's parallel
# workers); +0.75 and +1.5 = illustrative moderate/substantial in-situ
# fragmentation scenarios. Uses the *same* n_boot/sim/cv_uf/rmore_method as the
# production sediment call (Section 11.2/11.3) -- no analytical-budget change.
sed_psd_shift_grid <- c(0, 0.75, 1.5)

sed_psd_shift_tbl <- sediment_psd_shift_sensitivity(
  param_values_base = param_values_sed,
  slope_shift_grid  = sed_psd_shift_grid,
  tox_data_sed      = tox_data_sed,
  n_boot            = n_boot,
  cv_uf             = 0.5,
  rmore_method      = "lognormal",
  sim               = 30,
  num_cores         = parallel::detectCores() - 2,
  quantitative_flag = sediment_concentration_is_quantitative
)

    sediment_concentration_is_quantitative,

  )
)

sed_psd_shift_plot

Across the illustrative grid from no shift to the largest tested shift (1.5), the derived median Food Dilution HC5 changes by a factor of 0x and the Tissue Translocation HC5 by a factor of 0.42x (both relative to the unshifted grid point) — i.e., at this development-scale budget the rendered HC5 rose rather than fell as the illustrative PSD was shifted finer, the opposite of the direction the mechanism in Section 11.5.1 would naively suggest. This is read as evidence of SSD instability, not as a directional finding. The sediment benthic SSD is built from only 9 species; shifting which particles clear the ingestible/translocatable size gate can change which one or two species anchor the low-percentile HC5 extrapolation, and with this few species that anchor can swap non-monotonically rather than shift smoothly — exactly the small/unstable-SSD concern Thuy-Dung et al. (2026) raise as the motivation for tracking individual-species risk (Section 11.5.4) alongside a community HC5 extrapolated from so few species. This table and plot remain non-quantitative while sediment_concentration_is_quantitative is FALSE, regardless of direction: no number in this subsection should be combined with the Section 11.4 exposure figures to produce a sediment RQ, and the illustrative grid should not be read as showing that further fragmentation lowers sediment risk.

C.2 time-varying bioaccessibility (documented; future enhancement)

The existing pSSD++ bioaccessibility alignment already used throughout this report (food dilution → gut-volume alignment; translocation truncated at the 500 µm upper tissue-translocation limit, both inside run_pssd_pipeline()/PSSDplusplus::MC_sim_align_parallel()) is the same machinery this extension would reuse — it is a size-dependent gate, not a new framework. TODO (not implemented in this revision): make that gate explicitly time-dependent by (1) parameterizing the sediment PSD shift in Section 11.5.2 as a function of residence time t rather than an unordered scenario index (e.g., a size-shift schedule Δα(t) informed by, but not equal to, Thuy-Dung et al.’s doubling-time concept — explicitly not their prill-specific kfrag, per Section 11.5.2’s non-transplant note); (2) re-running run_pssd_pipeline() at each time step exactly as Section 11.5.2 already does at each scenario point, so smaller-mouthed/smaller-gut benthic species progressively clear the ingestible/translocatable size gate as the bed fragments; (3) reporting HC5(t) and, where a genuine sediment concentration becomes available (SPEC 1d), RCR(t), as a trajectory rather than a single value. This is left as a clearly-scoped TODO rather than implemented here because it requires a defensible time axis (a residence-time or age-of-deposition estimate for this sediment dataset) that does not currently exist in the source data — fabricating one would misrepresent the method’s evidentiary basis. Section 11.5.2’s scenario grid is the same computational step without the time axis, and can be converted into this trajectory once residence-time data are available.

This water-sediment comparison is interpretive inference, not a new correction. Under Hoffman et al. (2026), sediment and water PSDs may be linked by size sorting: loss of larger dense particles from the water column should correspond to sediment enrichment in those sizes. The plot and table are retained as a coherence check to guide future transport-correction work.

15.5 C1 number-snapshot guardrail

The C1 consolidation pass (structure/presentation only; see docs/CHANGELOG_hoffman_revisions.md) must not change any live number. This chunk captures every headline value the C1 spec designates as protected – river/sediment/ocean CF medians + 90% CIs, river/ocean EED q50/q95, the canonical 9-row C-PSD slope table, the SPEC Q1 max|delta a_cpsd|, the slope-structural-SD sensitivity grid, and river/ocean 1D + MC2D risk summaries – into data_output/c1_number_snapshot.json the first time it renders (file does not yet exist), and on every subsequent render re-derives the same values and asserts they still match that baseline within 1e-8 (exact equality for integers/n_bins). A failure here means a structural edit silently moved a number and must be treated as a stop-and-fix, not a value to update casually – see docs/CHANGELOG_hoffman_revisions.md before touching the baseline file itself.

Show the code 
c1_snapshot_path <- file.path(proj_root, "data_output", "c1_number_snapshot.json")

build_c1_snapshot <- function() {
  slope_tbl <- this_study_length_alpha |>
    dplyr::filter(Source == "This study matrix/shape") |>
    dplyr::arrange(PSD_ID) |>
    dplyr::transmute(
      PSD_ID, Matrix, Shape,
      a_cpsd = round(a_cpsd, 10), a_psd = round(a_psd, 10),
      lod_low_um = round(lod_low_um, 6), lod_high_um = round(lod_high_um, 6),
      n_bins = as.integer(n_bins)
    )

  rq_tbl <- function(x) x |> dplyr::arrange(ERM, HCx) |>
    dplyr::transmute(ERM, HCx, P_exceed = round(P_exceed, 10),
                      RQ_p50 = round(RQ_p50, 10), RQ_p95 = round(RQ_p95, 10))

  mc2d_tbl <- function(x) x |> dplyr::arrange(ERM, HCx) |>
    dplyr::transmute(ERM, HCx, P_exceed_med = round(P_exceed_med, 10),
                      RQ_p50_med = round(RQ_p50_med, 10), RQ_p95_med = round(RQ_p95_med, 10))

  list(
    cf_river  = list(p50 = unname(round(median(combined_cf), 10)),
                      p05 = unname(round(quantile(combined_cf, 0.05), 10)),
                      p95 = unname(round(quantile(combined_cf, 0.95), 10))),
    cf_sed    = list(p50 = unname(round(median(combined_cf_sed), 10)),
                      p05 = unname(round(quantile(combined_cf_sed, 0.05), 10)),
                      p95 = unname(round(quantile(combined_cf_sed, 0.95), 10))),
    cf_ocean  = list(p50 = unname(round(median(combined_cf_ocean), 10)),
                      p05 = unname(round(quantile(combined_cf_ocean, 0.05), 10)),
                      p95 = unname(round(quantile(combined_cf_ocean, 0.95), 10))),
    eed_river = list(q50 = unname(round(median(eed_boot$q50), 10)),
                      q95 = unname(round(median(eed_boot$q95), 10))),
    eed_ocean = list(q50 = unname(round(median(eed_boot_ocean$q50), 10)),
                      q95 = unname(round(median(eed_boot_ocean$q95), 10))),
    slope_table         = slope_tbl,
    spec_q1_max_delta    = unname(round(q1_max_abs_delta_a_cpsd, 10)),
    hoffman_sensitivity = hoffman_slope_sensitivity |>
      dplyr::arrange(structural_sd, ERM) |>
      dplyr::transmute(ERM, structural_sd, P_exceed_med = round(P_exceed_med, 10),
                        RQ_p50_med = round(RQ_p50_med, 10), RQ_p95_med = round(RQ_p95_med, 10)),
    rq_1d_river  = rq_tbl(risk_summary),
    rq_1d_sed    = rq_tbl(risk_summary_sed),
    rq_1d_ocean  = rq_tbl(risk_summary_ocean),
    mc2d_river   = mc2d_tbl(mc2d_summary),
    mc2d_ocean   = mc2d_tbl(mc2d_ocean_summary)
  )
}

snap_current <- build_c1_snapshot()

if (n_boot < 1000) {
  message("C1 guardrail: SKIPPED -- n_boot = ", n_boot, " (< 1000, dev-scale iteration render). ",
          "The byte-identical number check is only meaningful at the production budget; ",
          "re-render with n_boot = 1000 before treating this as a release-gate pass.")
} else if (!file.exists(c1_snapshot_path)) {
  jsonlite::write_json(snap_current, c1_snapshot_path, auto_unbox = TRUE, digits = 15, pretty = TRUE)
  message("C1 guardrail: baseline snapshot written to ", c1_snapshot_path,
          " (this is the pre-C1 baseline -- do not regenerate once C1 edits begin).")
} else {
  snap_baseline <- jsonlite::read_json(c1_snapshot_path, simplifyVector = TRUE)

  compare_numeric <- function(cur, base, path = "") {
    if (is.list(cur) && !is.data.frame(cur)) {
      nm <- names(cur)
      unlist(lapply(nm, function(n) compare_numeric(cur[[n]], base[[n]], paste0(path, "$", n))))
    } else if (is.data.frame(cur)) {
      base_df <- as.data.frame(base)
      stopifnot2 <- vapply(setdiff(names(cur), c("PSD_ID","Matrix","Shape","ERM","HCx")), function(col) {
        max(abs(cur[[col]] - base_df[[col]]), na.rm = TRUE)
      }, numeric(1))
      setNames(stopifnot2, paste0(path, "$", names(stopifnot2)))
    } else {
      setNames(abs(as.numeric(cur) - as.numeric(base)), path)
    }
  }

  diffs <- unlist(compare_numeric(snap_current, snap_baseline))
  tol <- 1e-8
  bad <- diffs[!is.na(diffs) & diffs >= tol]

  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    print(sort(bad, decreasing = TRUE))
    # Diagnostic print() output can be lost if the render halts before the
    # chunk's buffer flushes; also write it to a plain file so a failure is
    # debuggable from the last render alone.
    writeLines(
      c(paste0("C1 guardrail FAILURE -- ", length(bad), " value(s) exceeded tol = ", tol),
        capture.output(print(sort(bad, decreasing = TRUE))),
        "",
        "-- current --",
        capture.output(str(snap_current, max.level = 2)),
        "",
        "-- baseline --",
        capture.output(str(snap_baseline, max.level = 2))),
      file.path(proj_root, "data_output", "c1_guardrail_failure_diagnostic.txt")
    )
  }
  message("C1 guardrail: max|delta| across ", length(diffs), " tracked values = ",
          format(max(diffs, na.rm = TRUE), scientific = TRUE))
  stopifnot(
    "C1 guardrail FAILED: a structural edit changed a protected number -- see printed diagnostic above" =
      length(bad) == 0
  )
  message("C1 guardrail: all tracked values match the pre-C1 baseline within ", tol, ".")
}

16.1 SI Tables S5–S11: particle properties, fit statistics, and concentration rescaling

Supplementary tables reporting the particle properties underlying, the fitted parameters and fit statistics of every particle-size probability distribution fitted in this report, and the concentration rescaling for every monitoring sample, formatted after Kooi et al. (2021, Water Research 202:117429, SI Tables S3–S4). River water (freshwater) is reported separately (Tables S5, S7) from ocean water and beach sand (Tables S6, S8). Table S9 provides every sample’s location, PSD model, slope, correction factor, and rescaled concentration; river samples appear under both river-specific and pooled-river scenarios. Table S10 summarizes those values by matrix and PSD model, and Table S11 additionally breaks them down by location. Ocean-water and beach-sand samples are shown under their available pooled-matrix model. Each C-PSD row reports the fitted window [xmin, xmax) selected by the Segur et al. (2026) two-step LOD algorithm (or fixed by the length/width-consistent volume bounds, Section 4.2.3; area fits use a fixed lower search bound, Section 4.2.2), the cumulative slope αCPSD and log10 intercept b of log10 N(≥x) = b + αCPSD log10 x (± OLS standard error), the differential BN-PSD slope aPSD = αCPSD − 1 (same SE; the Kooi et al. positive PDF exponent is α = |aPSD|), R², and the number of populated bins fitted. Lower/upper quartiles are the 25th/75th percentiles. Mass is volume × polymer-resolved density (Section 3.1.1), reported in µg. Fits are summarized from the fit objects above, not refit – except the depth-stratified river length fits, which are deterministically refit here (identical call to Section 10.0) to retain intercepts and bin counts, and checked against depth_shape_fits.

Show the code 
source(file.path(proj_root, "R", "si_pdf_tables.R"))

# ---- Particle properties (Kooi et al. 2021 Table S3 analogue) ----
si_props_river <- si_particle_properties(raw_particles_river, "River water")
si_props_ocean_sed <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  si_particle_properties(raw_particles_ocean, "Ocean water"),
  si_particle_properties(raw_particles_sed,   "Beach sand")
)

# ---- C-PSD fit parameters (Kooi et al. 2021 Table S4 analogue) ----
metric_spec <- list(
  Length = list(col = "length_um", bin = 5,          unit = "Length (µm)"),
  Area   = list(col = "area_um2",  bin = 500,        unit = "Projected area (µm²)"),
  Volume = list(col = "V_um3",     bin = vol_bin_um, unit = "Volume (µm³)")
)
pooled_rows <- function(fits_by_metric, df, matrix_label) {
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(fits_by_metric), function(m) {
    si_cpsd_fit_rows(fits_by_metric[[m]], df, metric_spec[[m]]$col, metric_spec[[m]]$bin,
                     matrix_label, metric_spec[[m]]$unit, "Pooled (all sites)")
  }))
}

# River: pooled, per-location (length/area/volume x shape), depth-stratified (length)
si_depth_fits <- si_depth_stratified_fits(raw_particles_river, depth_levels)
# The SI depth rows are C-PSD fits; Section 10.0 stores the headline estimator, so convert before comparing.
si_depth_headline_a <- function(d, shp) {
  f <- si_depth_fits[[d]][[shp]]
  if (!identical(slope_estimator, "tpl_mle")) return(f$a_cpsd)
  sub <- raw_particles_river[raw_particles_river$sample_depth_general == d, ]
  vals <- if (shp == "all") sub$length_um else sub$length_um[sub$shape == shp]
  as_headline_fit(f, vals, headline_length_window)$a_cpsd
}
depth_check <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(si_depth_fits), function(d)
  tibble::tibble(sample_depth_general = d, shape = names(si_depth_fits[[d]]),
                 a_cpsd_si = vapply(names(si_depth_fits[[d]]), function(s) si_depth_headline_a(d, s), numeric(1))))) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(depth_shape_fits, by = c("sample_depth_general", "shape"))
stopifnot("SI depth-stratified refit must reproduce Section 10.0 slopes" =
            nrow(depth_check) == nrow(depth_shape_fits) &&
            max(abs(depth_check$a_cpsd_si - depth_check$a_cpsd)) < 1e-12)

per_loc_fits <- list(Length = cpsd_loc_shape_length, Area = cpsd_loc_shape_area,
                     Volume = cpsd_loc_shape_vol)
si_fits_river <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  pooled_rows(list(Length = cpsd_fits_river_length, Area = cpsd_fits_river_area,
                   Volume = cpsd_fits_river_volume), raw_particles_river, "River water"),
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(per_loc_fits), function(m) {
    dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(per_loc_fits[[m]]), function(loc) {
      si_cpsd_fit_rows(per_loc_fits[[m]][[loc]],
                       dplyr::filter(raw_particles_river, sample_location == loc),
                       metric_spec[[m]]$col, metric_spec[[m]]$bin,
                       "River water", metric_spec[[m]]$unit, paste0("Site: ", loc))
    }))
  })),
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(si_depth_fits), function(d) {
    si_cpsd_fit_rows(si_depth_fits[[d]],
                     dplyr::filter(raw_particles_river, sample_depth_general == d),
                     "length_um", 5, "River water", "Length (µm)", paste0("Depth: ", d))
  }))
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(Metric = factor(Metric, levels = vapply(metric_spec, `[[`, "", "unit"))) |>
  dplyr::arrange(Metric) |>
  dplyr::mutate(Metric = as.character(Metric))

# Ocean water (pooled + per-coastal-site length) and beach sand (pooled)
si_fits_ocean_sed <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  pooled_rows(list(Length = cpsd_fits_ocean_length, Area = cpsd_fits_ocean_area,
                   Volume = cpsd_fits_ocean_volume), raw_particles_ocean, "Ocean water"),
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(cpsd_fits_ocean_by_loc), function(loc) {
    si_cpsd_fit_rows(list(all = cpsd_fits_ocean_by_loc[[loc]]),
                     dplyr::filter(raw_particles_ocean, sample_location == loc),
                     "length_um", 5, "Ocean water", "Length (µm)", paste0("Site: ", loc))
  })),
  pooled_rows(list(Length = cpsd_fits_sed_length, Area = cpsd_fits_sed_area,
                   Volume = cpsd_fits_sed_volume), raw_particles_sed, "Beach sand")
)

# ---- Alternative / structural models fitted to pooled particle length ----
si_alt_models <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  m13_fit_summary |>
    dplyr::transmute(
      Matrix, Model = "MLE power law (poweRlaw::conpl)",
      `x_min or break (µm)` = xmin_um, `n (tail or total)` = n_tail,
      Parameters = sprintf("α = %.3f", alpha_MLE),
      `Fit statistics` = sprintf("KS D = %.4f; bootstrap GOF p = %.2f", KS_D, bootstrap_p)
    ),
  m13_fit_summary |>
    dplyr::transmute(
      Matrix, Model = "Lognormal at MLE x_min (poweRlaw::conlnorm)",
      `x_min or break (µm)` = xmin_um, `n (tail or total)` = n_tail,
      Parameters = sprintf("meanlog = %.3f; sdlog = %.3f", lognormal_meanlog, lognormal_sdlog),
      `Fit statistics` = sprintf("Vuong R = %.3f; p = %.3f (vs. power law)", vuong_stat, vuong_p)
    ),
  critical_piecewise_tbl |>
    dplyr::transmute(
      Matrix, Model = "Two-segment C-PSD (piecewise OLS)",
      `x_min or break (µm)` = piecewise_break_um,
      `n (tail or total)` = NA_integer_,
      Parameters = sprintf("α_CPSD,low = %.2f; α_CPSD,high = %.2f", piecewise_low_a_cpsd, piecewise_high_a_cpsd),
      `Fit statistics` = sprintf("ΔAIC vs. single slope = %.1f", piecewise_delta_aic)
    )
)
si_alt_models <- si_alt_models |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    Matrix = dplyr::recode(Matrix, "Sediment" = "Beach sand"),
    `n (tail or total)` = ifelse(is.na(`n (tail or total)`), "–", as.character(`n (tail or total)`))
  )
si_alt_models_river     <- dplyr::filter(si_alt_models, Matrix == "River water")
si_alt_models_ocean_sed <- dplyr::filter(si_alt_models, Matrix != "River water") |>
  dplyr::arrange(factor(Matrix, levels = c("Ocean water", "Beach sand")))

# ---- Existing production and pooled concentration-rescaling outputs (Tables S9-S11) ----
monitoring_river_specific_si <- monitoring |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    a_psd_default = if (use_river_slopes) {
      vapply(as.character(river), function(location) {
        cpsd_fits_by_loc[[location]]$a_psd
      }, numeric(1))
    } else {
      rep(cpsd_fit_all$a_psd, dplyr::n())
    }
  )
monitoring_river_pooled_si <- river_corr_pooled$monitoring |>
  dplyr::mutate(a_psd_default = cpsd_fit_all$a_psd)
monitoring_sed_si <- monitoring_sed |>
  dplyr::mutate(a_psd_default = cpsd_fit_sed_all$a_psd)
monitoring_ocean_si <- monitoring_ocean |>
  dplyr::mutate(a_psd_default = cpsd_fit_ocean_all$a_psd)

si_rescaling_samples <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  si_rescaling_sample_rows(
    monitoring_river_specific_si, C_corrected_draws, "C_measured_pL", "River water",
    "particles/L", psd_model = "River-specific", location_col = "river"
  ),
  si_rescaling_sample_rows(
    monitoring_river_pooled_si, river_corr_pooled$C_corrected_draws, "C_measured_pL", "River water",
    "particles/L", psd_model = "Pooled", location_col = "river"
  ),
  si_rescaling_sample_rows(
    monitoring_ocean_si, C_corrected_draws_ocean, "C_measured_pL", "Ocean water",
    "particles/L", psd_model = "Pooled", location_col = "sample_location"
  ),
  si_rescaling_sample_rows(
    monitoring_sed_si, C_corrected_draws_sed, "C_measured_pkg", "Beach sand",
    "particles/L", psd_model = "Pooled", location_col = "sample_location"
  )
) |>
  dplyr::arrange(
    factor(Matrix, levels = c("River water", "Ocean water", "Beach sand")),
    Location,
    `Sample ID`,
    factor(`PSD model`, levels = c("River-specific", "Pooled"))
  )
stopifnot(
  nrow(si_rescaling_samples) == 2 * nrow(monitoring) + nrow(monitoring_ocean) + nrow(monitoring_sed),
  all(!is.na(si_rescaling_samples$Location)),
  all(!is.na(si_rescaling_samples$`PSD model`)),
  all(is.finite(si_rescaling_samples$`CF (median)`)),
  all(is.finite(si_rescaling_samples$`Reported concentration (median)`)),
  all(is.finite(si_rescaling_samples$`Fit-window concentration (median)`)),
  all(is.finite(si_rescaling_samples$`Rescaled concentration (median)`))
)
si_rescaling_summary <- si_rescaling_matrix_summary(
  si_rescaling_samples,
  group_cols = c("Matrix", "PSD model", "Concentration unit")
)
si_rescaling_location_summary <- si_rescaling_matrix_summary(
  si_rescaling_samples,
  group_cols = c("Matrix", "Location", "PSD model", "Concentration unit")
)

# Full-precision numeric versions (formatted versions go to the manuscript workbook)
si_csv_dir <- file.path(proj_root, "data_output", "si_pdf_tables")
dir.create(si_csv_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
for (nm in c("si_props_river", "si_props_ocean_sed", "si_fits_river", "si_fits_ocean_sed",
             "si_rescaling_samples", "si_rescaling_summary", "si_rescaling_location_summary")) {
  utils::write.csv(get(nm), file.path(si_csv_dir, paste0(nm, ".csv")), row.names = FALSE,
                   fileEncoding = "UTF-8")
}

# Word version of Tables S5-S11, with a variable-definitions section
# ---- Headline fixed-window MLE fits (Table S7c) ----
si_headline_tbl <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  si_headline_fit_rows(list(all = cpsd_fit_all, fragment = cpsd_fit_frag, fiber = cpsd_fit_fiber), "River water", "Length (µm)", "Pooled (all sites)"),
  si_headline_fit_rows(list(all = cpsd_fit_area, fragment = cpsd_fit_area_fragment, fiber = cpsd_fit_area_fiber), "River water", "Projected area (µm²)", "Pooled (all sites)"),
  si_headline_fit_rows(list(all = cpsd_fit_volume, fragment = cpsd_fit_volume_fragment, fiber = cpsd_fit_volume_fiber), "River water", "Volume (µm³)", "Pooled (all sites)"),
  dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(cpsd_loc_shape_length), function(loc) dplyr::bind_rows(
    si_headline_fit_rows(cpsd_loc_shape_length[[loc]]["all"], "River water", "Length (µm)", paste0("Site: ", loc)),
    si_headline_fit_rows(cpsd_loc_shape_area[[loc]]["all"], "River water", "Projected area (µm²)", paste0("Site: ", loc)),
    si_headline_fit_rows(cpsd_loc_shape_vol[[loc]]["all"], "River water", "Volume (µm³)", paste0("Site: ", loc))))),
  si_headline_fit_rows(list(all = cpsd_fit_ocean_all, fragment = cpsd_fit_ocean_frag, fiber = cpsd_fit_ocean_fiber), "Ocean water", "Length (µm)", "Pooled (all sites)"),
  si_headline_fit_rows(list(all = cpsd_fit_area_ocean), "Ocean water", "Projected area (µm²)", "Pooled (all sites)"),
  si_headline_fit_rows(list(all = cpsd_fit_volume_ocean), "Ocean water", "Volume (µm³)", "Pooled (all sites)"),
  si_headline_fit_rows(list(all = cpsd_fit_sed_all, fragment = cpsd_fit_sed_frag, fiber = cpsd_fit_sed_fiber), "Beach sand", "Length (µm)", "Pooled (all sites)"),
  si_headline_fit_rows(list(all = cpsd_fit_area_sed), "Beach sand", "Projected area (µm²)", "Pooled (all sites)"),
  si_headline_fit_rows(list(all = cpsd_fit_volume_sed), "Beach sand", "Volume (µm³)", "Pooled (all sites)"))
utils::write.csv(si_headline_tbl, file.path(si_csv_dir, "si_headline_fits.csv"), row.names = FALSE, fileEncoding = "UTF-8")

)

}

17. Single-matrix variants of multi-matrix figures

Every figure above that overlays two or more matrices (river, ocean, sediment) in one panel is reproduced here as separate single-matrix variants – river-only, ocean-only, and/or sediment-only, whichever matrices that particular figure actually contains. Each variant reuses the exact data and geometry of its combined source figure, filtered to one matrix, and is saved alongside the original under a _river/_ocean/_sediment filename suffix. Matrices that a given combined figure never included (e.g., sediment in the river/ocean-only comparisons below) have no corresponding variant produced, rather than a fabricated empty one.

17.1 Figure 1 / cpsd_river_ocean_facet_plot (river, ocean)

Show the code 
build_cpsd_river_ocean_variant <- function(sel_locations, mat_label) {
  pts <- dplyr::filter(cpsd_loc_points_ro, location %in% sel_locations)
  lns <- dplyr::filter(cpsd_loc_lines_ro,  location %in% sel_locations)
  pal <- loc_palette_ro_used[names(loc_palette_ro_used) %in% sel_locations]

  p <- ggplot2::ggplot() +
    ggplot2::geom_point(
      data = dplyr::filter(pts, !in_lod),
      ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), y = logN, color = location),
      size = 0.7, alpha = 0.05, shape = 16
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_point(
      data = dplyr::filter(pts, in_lod),
      ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), y = logN, color = location),
      size = 1.3, alpha = 0.75, shape = 16
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_ribbon(
      data = lns, ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), ymin = logN_lo, ymax = logN_hi, fill = location),
      alpha = 0.12, color = NA
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_line(
      data = lns, ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), y = logN_fit, color = location),
      linewidth = 0.9, alpha = 0.9
    ) +
    ggplot2::facet_grid(shape ~ metric, scales = "free_x", labeller = ggplot2::label_value) +
    ggplot2::coord_cartesian(ylim = y_range_ro) +
    ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = int_breaks, labels = function(x) round(x)) +
    ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(breaks = int_breaks, labels = function(x) round(x)) +
    ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = pal, name = NULL) +
    ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = pal, guide = "none") +
    ggplot2::guides(color = ggplot2::guide_legend(override.aes = list(alpha = 1, size = 3))) +
    ggplot2::labs(
      x = expression(log[10] * "(size)"), y = expression(log[10] * (N("">=L))),
      title    = paste0("Power-law fits (headline fixed-window MLE) — ", mat_label, " only, by shape and size metric"),
      subtitle = "Solid lines + ribbon = fit ± 95% CI within the fit window. Faded points = outside the window."
    ) +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 18) +
    ggplot2::theme(
      legend.position = "bottom",
      panel.border    = ggplot2::element_rect(color = "gray80", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.4),
      strip.text      = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", size = 10)
    )

  ggsave(p, filename = paste0("figures/cpsd_river_ocean_facet_plot_", tolower(mat_label), ".png"),
         width = 12, height = 8, dpi = 300)
  p
}

build_cpsd_river_ocean_variant(locations, "river")

build_slopes_metrics_variant <- function(mat) {
  dat <- dplyr::filter(matrix_slopes_all_metrics, matrix == mat)
  p <- ggplot2::ggplot(dat, ggplot2::aes(x = group, y = a_cpsd, color = matrix)) +
    ggplot2::geom_point(size = 4) +
    ggplot2::geom_errorbar(
      ggplot2::aes(ymin = a_cpsd - se_a_cpsd, ymax = a_cpsd + se_a_cpsd), width = 0.2, linewidth = 0.8
    ) +
    ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ metric, nrow = 1) +
    ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = matrix_pal_slopes, guide = "none") +
    ggplot2::labs(
      x = if (mat == "River") "River location" else NULL,
      y = expression(italic(a)[cpsd]),
      title    = paste0("Headline slope by size metric — ", mat, " only"),
      subtitle = "Error bars = ±1 SE."
    ) +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 20) +
    ggplot2::theme(
      panel.border = ggplot2::element_rect(color = "gray85", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.4),
      strip.text   = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold"),
      axis.text.x  = ggplot2::element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
    )
  ggsave(p, filename = paste0("figures/cpsd_slopes_all_metrics_plot_", tolower(mat), ".png"),
         width = 9, height = 6, dpi = 300)
  p
}

build_single_vs_piecewise_variant <- function(mat) {
  df_f             <- dplyr::filter(df_both_ms,        Matrix == mat)
  pred_single_f    <- dplyr::filter(pred_single_ms,     Matrix == mat)
  pred_piecewise_f <- dplyr::filter(pred_piecewise_ms,  Matrix == mat)
  lod_f            <- dplyr::filter(lod_bounds_both_ms, Matrix == mat)

  p <- ggplot2::ggplot(df_f, ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), y = log10(N_ge), color = Matrix)) +
    ggplot2::geom_vline(
      data = lod_f, ggplot2::aes(xintercept = xval),
      linetype = "dotted", color = "gray55", linewidth = 0.6, inherit.aes = FALSE
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(alpha = in_lod), size = 1.3) +
    ggplot2::geom_ribbon(
      data = pred_single_f, ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), ymin = logN_lo, ymax = logN_hi),
      inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = unname(matrix_pal_cpsd[mat]), alpha = 0.15
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_ribbon(
      data = pred_piecewise_f, ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), ymin = logN_lo, ymax = logN_hi, group = segment),
      inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = unname(matrix_pal_cpsd[mat]), alpha = 0.15
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_line(
      data = pred_single_f, ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), y = logN_fit),
      inherit.aes = FALSE, color = "grey15", alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 2.6
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_line(
      data = pred_single_f, ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), y = logN_fit, color = I(line_color)),
      inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 1.4
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_line(
      data = pred_piecewise_f, ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), y = logN_fit, group = segment),
      inherit.aes = FALSE, color = "grey15", alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 2.6
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_line(
      data = pred_piecewise_f, ggplot2::aes(x = log10(L_low), y = logN_fit, color = I(line_color), group = segment),
      inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 1.4
    ) +
    ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ Model, nrow = 1) +
    ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = matrix_pal_cpsd, guide = "none") +
    ggplot2::scale_alpha_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 0.5, `FALSE` = 0.10), guide = "none") +
    ggplot2::labs(
      title    = paste0("Single-slope (headline MLE) vs. two-segment fit — ", mat, " only (particle length)"),
      subtitle = "Dotted = fitted LOD window boundaries. Faded points = outside LOD window.",
      x        = expression(log[10] * "(Length, " * mu * "m)"),
      y        = expression(log[10] * (N("">=L)))
    ) +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
    ggplot2::theme(
      strip.text   = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
      panel.border = ggplot2::element_rect(color = "gray80", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.4)
    )
  fname <- paste0("figures/cpsd_single_vs_piecewise_plot_", tolower(gsub(" water", "", mat)), ".png")
  ggsave(p, filename = fname, width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 300)
  p
}

    ggplot2::geom_errorbar(

build_cf_bounding_variant <- function(mat) {
  dat <- cf_bounding_tbl |>
    dplyr::filter(Matrix == mat) |>
    dplyr::select(Matrix, `Single-slope (production)` = CF_single_slope_p50, `Piecewise (bounding)` = CF_piecewise) |>
    tidyr::pivot_longer(-Matrix, names_to = "Case", values_to = "CF") |>
    dplyr::mutate(Case = factor(Case, levels = c("Single-slope (production)", "Piecewise (bounding)")))

  p <- ggplot2::ggplot(dat, ggplot2::aes(x = Case, y = CF, color = Case)) +
    ggplot2::geom_line(ggplot2::aes(group = Matrix), color = "gray70", linewidth = 0.6) +
    ggplot2::geom_point(size = 4) +
    ggplot2::scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_number()) +
    ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = c("Single-slope (production)" = "#009E73", "Piecewise (bounding)" = "#D55E00"), guide = "none") +
    ggplot2::labs(
      x = NULL, y = "Correction factor (median) [log10 scale]",
      title = paste0("Single-slope vs. piecewise correction factor — ", mat, " only")
    ) +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
    ggplot2::theme(panel.border = ggplot2::element_rect(color = "gray80", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.4))
  ggsave(p, filename = paste0("figures/cf_bounding_plot_", tolower(gsub(" water", "", mat)), ".png"),
         width = 6, height = 5.5, dpi = 300)
  p
}

17.7 Figure S7 / alpha_comparison_plot (river/freshwater, ocean/marine)

Sediment is not part of this literature comparison at all (Methods, Section 2.3), so only river (Freshwater) and ocean (Marine) variants are produced. Zhao et al. (2026)’s pooled freshwater+marine meta-analysis point is, by its own source paper, not separable into a matrix and so does not appear in either single-matrix variant – consistent with the combined figure already labeling it “Mixed (unclassified)” rather than assigning it to one matrix.

Show the code 
build_alpha_forest_variant <- function(mat, mat_label) {
  dat <- alpha_forest_df |>
    dplyr::filter(Matrix == mat) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      Source = factor(as.character(Source), levels = intersect(source_levels_bottom_to_top, as.character(Source))),
      x_pos  = as.numeric(Source) + offset
    )
  src_levels <- levels(dat$Source)

  p <- ggplot2::ggplot(dat, ggplot2::aes(x = x_pos, y = alpha_abs)) +
    ggplot2::geom_boxplot(
      data = dplyr::filter(dat, is_boxplot_row),
      ggplot2::aes(group = Source, fill = Matrix),
      color = "#009E73", alpha = 0.12, width = 0.55, outlier.shape = NA
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_errorbar(
      data = dplyr::filter(dat, !is.na(se)),
      ggplot2::aes(ymin = alpha_abs - ci_mult * se, ymax = alpha_abs + ci_mult * se, color = Matrix),
      width = 0.10, linewidth = 0.6
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_jitter(
      data = dplyr::filter(dat, is_boxplot_row),
      ggplot2::aes(color = Matrix, shape = Shape),
      width = 0.24, height = 0, alpha = 0.35, size = 1.6
    ) +
    ggplot2::geom_point(
      data = dplyr::filter(dat, !is_boxplot_row),
      ggplot2::aes(color = Matrix, shape = Shape),
      size = 3.2, alpha = 0.95
    ) +
    ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
      data = dplyr::filter(dat, !is.na(point_label)),
      ggplot2::aes(label = point_label),
      size = 3.0, max.overlaps = Inf, show.legend = FALSE,
      box.padding = 0.4, point.padding = 0.2, force = 2, force_pull = 0.5,
      min.segment.length = 0, segment.size = 0.3, segment.alpha = 0.5, seed = 1
    ) +
    ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = matrix_pal_forest, drop = FALSE, guide = "none") +
    ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = matrix_pal_forest, drop = FALSE, guide = "none") +
    ggplot2::scale_shape_manual(values = shape_pal_forest, name = "Shape", drop = FALSE) +
    ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(
      breaks = seq_along(src_levels),
      labels = stringr::str_wrap(unname(source_labels_clean[src_levels]), width = 40),
      expand = ggplot2::expansion(add = 0.6)
    ) +
    ggplot2::coord_flip() +
    ggplot2::labs(
      x = NULL,
      y = expression("|" * italic(a)[psd] * "| from particle-length PSD"),
      shape = "Shape",
      title    = paste0(mat_label, "-only particle-length PSD slopes: this study vs. literature"),
      subtitle = "This study retains the fragment/fiber/all shape distinction; error bars per source as in the combined figure (Figure S7)."
    ) +
    ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
    ggplot2::theme(
      axis.text.y  = ggplot2::element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
      legend.position = "right",
      panel.border = ggplot2::element_rect(color = "gray82", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.4),
      plot.title   = ggplot2::element_text(size = 15),
      plot.subtitle = ggplot2::element_text(size = 10.5, color = "gray30")
    )
  ggsave(p, filename = paste0("figures/alpha_comparison_plot_", tolower(mat_label), ".png"),
         width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 300)
  p
}

Appendix M. Manuscript parameter export (single source of truth)

Every PSD, rescaling and risk number quoted in the Savoca et al. manuscript and SI is written here to data_output/psd_rescaling_params.json (and a flat CSV), at full precision, from the objects computed above. Rounding happens only in the manuscript-generation step. W1 values use the resolved rescaling basis: concentrations restricted to the fixed fit window, rescaled with each river’s own fixed-window MLE slope (pooled slope, two-segment model and the former C-PSD slopes as sensitivities). W2 is the reported 50–500 µm concentration.

                            CI95_a_diff = f$a_psd + c(-1.96, 1.96) * f$se_a_psd, R2 = f$r2, n_bins = .nb(f),

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo    = TRUE,
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  fig.width  = 9,
  fig.height = 6
)

set.seed(1)

# Prevent knitr's inline-r hook from rendering large legacy-slope RQ/CF values
# (e.g. ~1e7 under the pre-fix cumulative volume slope, SPEC 1b) as mangled
# unrendered scientific notation (literal "1.2^{7}" text); does not change any
# computed value, only how numbers print.
options(scipen = 999)

# During an actual render (quarto render / rmarkdown::render()), knitr's working
# directory for THIS chunk is the .qmd's own directory (R/), but that can vary by
# how the render is invoked. Resolve the project root from the file's own known
# location via knitr::current_input() rather than assuming a starting cwd, so this
# works the same whether rendered from the project root, from R/, or via Quarto's
# CLI. Falls back to the current directory when run interactively (chunk-by-chunk),
# where cwd is normally already the project root.
proj_root <- tryCatch({
  doc_path <- knitr::current_input(dir = TRUE)
  if (is.null(doc_path) || !nzchar(doc_path)) stop("not knitting")
  normalizePath(file.path(dirname(doc_path), ".."))
}, error = function(e) normalizePath("."))

knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = proj_root)
getwd()

# ── Global Monte Carlo settings (change here to scale up/down) ──
# Budget is a document parameter: "production" for publication numbers,
# "quick" for fast iteration (everything self-labels via is_production_budget).
run_budget <- if (exists("params") && !is.null(params$budget)) params$budget else Sys.getenv("W2W_BUDGET", "production")
stopifnot(run_budget %in% c("production", "quick"))
n_boot <- if (identical(run_budget, "quick")) 100  else 1000   # bootstrap replicates (>= 1000 for publication)
n_mc   <- if (identical(run_budget, "quick")) 5000 else 20000  # alpha Monte Carlo draws

# C1.10: whether this render is at the production Monte Carlo budget (>= 1000
# bootstrap replicates) rather than a fast dev-scale iteration render. Derived
# from n_boot (not a separate hardcoded flag) so it can never drift out of
# sync with what was actually run. The report body states its numbers once,
# without "development-scale"/"re-check at full budget" hedges, because
# n_boot = 1000 is the confirmed production budget (not a placeholder); this
# flag exists so a future dev-scale iteration render (n_boot < 1000, faster
# turnaround while editing) is still self-labeled rather than silently
# passing off partial-budget numbers as final.
is_production_budget <- n_boot >= 1000

# Uniform C-PSD bin width for volume fits (µm³), applied identically across every
# matrix and shape (river/sediment/ocean; fragment/fiber/all) — the same convention
# already used for length (bin_um = 5 µm, fixed) and area (bin_um = 500 µm², fixed)
# fits below. Segur et al. (2026) demonstrate the C-PSD method's slope estimate
# should be ~bin-size-independent (RSD < 1.8%) *once the fit window is held fixed*;
# empirical testing here confirms that holds for volume too (RSD ~5-10% across a
# 10x range of bin_um) as long as the window itself isn't also re-optimized per bin
# size — see the volume-lod-bounds chunks below for why the window is fixed via
# length/width-consistent bounds rather than left to auto-detection for volume.
vol_bin_um <- 2e4

# Cache-invalidation key for the C-PSD fitting chunks below (cache=TRUE): any
# change to the underlying raw particle-measurement file bumps this value,
# which is included in each cached chunk's cache.extra, so every cached
# C-PSD fit is invalidated together on a real data change without needing
# per-chunk dependson wiring across river/sediment/ocean/per-location fits.
# Canonical per-sample monitoring table: the data owner's final QC'd summary
# (Part_dets_summ_final.rds; reproduces manuscript Table 1 exactly: 57 river
# samples, 3,777 particles). Sample-ID corrections follow Util_MSS.R.
monitoring_file <- file.path(proj_root, "data_input", "Part_dets_summ_final.rds")
monitoring_raw  <- readRDS(monitoring_file) |>
  dplyr::mutate(Client_ID_MSSupdate = dplyr::recode(Client_ID_MSSupdate,
                                                    "CR020250611S"    = "CR020250611SS",
                                                    "SRR20240205SS_2" = "SRR20240205SS"))
# ── Utility functions (sourced from companion scripts in R/) ──
# mp_risk_utils.R – C-PSD fitting, exposure/hazard/risk functions
# cpsd_plotting.R – plot_cpsd_multi(), MP_PALETTE
source(file.path(proj_root, "R", "mp_risk_utils.R"))
source(file.path(proj_root, "R", "cpsd_plotting.R"))
source(file.path(proj_root, "R", "risk_plotting.R"))    # matrix-aware risk plotting helpers

# Concentration basis for the C-PSD-window exposure concentration (see
# lod_scope_monitoring_concentrations()): "particle_rebuild" (production since
# 2026-10-15; QC-passing particle rows x summary aliquot factor
# extrap_count/count) or "reported_fraction" (reported concentration x in-window
# particle fraction; prior production, retained as a sensitivity).
# FLAG: the particle-rebuild basis needs data-owner confirmation before
# publication -- the summary's `count` cannot be reproduced from the particle
# table (data_output/particle_qc_reconciliation_by_sample.csv).
concentration_basis <- "particle_rebuild"

# Cache key: content hashes (not mtimes) of both input files, plus hashes of the
# spectral-QC rule and concentration basis. The particle-set hash is appended in
# Section 3.1 once the QC'd particle table exists, so every cached chunk below
# is invalidated by any change to the data, the QC filter, or the retained set.
# Headline power-law slope estimator (Section 4.1 and 13.7): "tpl_mle" = doubly
# truncated power-law maximum likelihood on the unbinned particle measurements
# within a window fixed in advance (production since 2026-10-15); "cpsd" = the
# Segur et al. (2026) cumulative-PSD regression (prior production, now a
# sensitivity). Length window: 100 um (reliable uFTIR detection at 25 um
# pixels, Section 10.2) to 500 um (sieve boundary, above which large particles
# are undercounted). Area and volume windows are implied by the length window.
slope_estimator <- "tpl_mle"
headline_length_window <- c(100, 500)

raw_data_cache_key <- list(
  particle_file = unname(tools::md5sum(file.path(proj_root, "data_input", "Part_dets_comb.rds"))),
  monitoring_file = unname(tools::md5sum(monitoring_file)),
  qc_filter = rlang::hash(deparse(spectra_qc_pass)),
  concentration_basis = concentration_basis,
  slope_estimator = slope_estimator,
  headline_length_window = headline_length_window,
  estimator_code = rlang::hash(list(deparse(tpl_mle), deparse(as_headline_fit))))

# Hoffman et al. (2026)-motivated sensitivity controls. These are explicit
# assumptions so they can be changed without editing hidden model logic.
slope_structural_sd <- 0.25
# River-water exposure rescaling: apply each river's own headline slope (and fit
# window) to that river's samples ("river", default), or one pooled slope to
# all samples ("pooled", retained as a sensitivity). River slopes differ
# significantly (Cochran's Q, Section 4.2.2), so pooling is not the default.
# Hazard-side alignment (pSSD++) still uses the pooled slope (alpha_mu/alpha_se).
slope_application   <- "river"
hoffman_delta_m     <- 0.10
hoffman_K_m2_s      <- 1e-5
polymer_density_tbl <- polymer_density_lookup()

# ── Additional packages used in plots ──
if (!requireNamespace("ggrepel",  quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("ggrepel")
if (!requireNamespace("scales",   quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("scales")
if (!requireNamespace("poweRlaw", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("poweRlaw")
library(ggrepel)
library(scales)
library(poweRlaw)
```

# 1. Overview

This document presents an **end-to-end, fully probabilistic** environmental risk assessment (ERA) workflow for microplastics in freshwater surface water and sediment from four central California rivers (Carmel, Pajaro, Salinas, and San Lorenzo). The workflow proceeds through five steps:

1. **Raw particle data → power-law slope** — maximum likelihood on the individual particle sizes, for a power law truncated at both ends of a fixed 100–500 µm window (headline; [Clauset et al. 2009](https://doi.org/10.1137/070710111); [Edwards et al. 2017](https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.12641)). The cumulative-PSD (C-PSD) fit of [Segur et al. (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1186/s43591-026-00205-5) is also reported, for comparison and as a sensitivity (Sections 4 and 13.7).
2. **Monitoring concentrations → probabilistic rescaling** — power-law integration converts measurements from a sampled size range to a target range, propagating slope uncertainty via Monte Carlo ([Coffin et al. 2022](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2022.155859)).
3. **Environmental Exposure Distribution (EED)** — nonparametric bootstrap of corrected site-level concentrations.
4. **Hazard threshold distribution** — probabilistic species sensitivity distributions (pSSD++) using the [PSSDplusplus R package](https://github.com/ScottCoffin/ToMEx2.0_EcoToxRisk/tree/main/package) and [ToMEx 2.0 toxicity database](https://github.com/ScottCoffin/ToMEx2.0_EcoToxRisk).
5. **Risk characterization** — Monte Carlo pairing of exposure and hazard distributions, expressed as risk quotient (RQ = Exposure/Hazard) and exceedance probability P(RQ > 1).

All custom R functions (`fit_cpsd_segur_r`, `correction_factor`, `bootstrap_eed`, `mc2d_risk`, etc.) live in `R/mp_risk_utils.R` and `R/cpsd_plotting.R` for reuse and eventual integration into **PSSDplusplus**. The Segur et al. (2026) LOD-detection algorithm is implemented directly in `R/mp_risk_utils.R` as pure R.

**Methodological basis.** This assessment treats the C-PSD slope convention, transport-induced slope structure, sampling depth, polymer density, and water-sediment PSD coherence as explicit, quantified uncertainty sources. Both the exposure-side correction factor and the hazard-side particle-trait alignment inside pSSD++ (length, area, volume, mass) integrate the **differential** PSD slope (*a*~psd~ = *a*~cpsd~ − 1), locked by a rendered worked-example assertion in Section 5.1.0 (Koelmans et al. 2020: CF = 8.32 for 30–2000 µm → 1–5000 µm at α = 1.6). Sediment (beach sand) is retained as an illustrative/methods demonstration only and excluded from the headline risk conclusion: its exposure concentration is a per-liter water value with no dry-mass basis, not a genuine particles/kg-dry-weight measurement (Section 11). Sediment is additionally framed as a time-dependent, accumulating compartment in which deposited microplastics continue to fragment in place, so any single-time-point sediment metric is a lower-bound snapshot ([Thuy-Dung, Groenenberg & Koelmans 2026](https://doi.org/10.1186/s43591-026-00210-8); Section 11) — a framing/sensitivity addition, not a re-introduction of sediment into the headline conclusion. The full revision history behind these corrections (prior convention errors and their quantified before/after effect) is in Appendix A and `docs/CHANGELOG_hoffman_revisions.md`. **Results at a glance** (river/ocean headline RQ, piecewise bound, sediment exclusion) follows Section 12; the fully quantified executive summary is in Key Findings.

# 2. Packages

```{r}
pkgs <- c("tidyverse", "truncnorm", "fitdistrplus", "ggpubr", "readxl")

if (length(to_install) > 0) install.packages(to_install)
lapply(pkgs, library, character.only = TRUE)

# pSSD++ package (GitHub)

# install from github unless library(PSSDplusplus) is not already installed
if (!requireNamespace("PSSDplusplus", quietly = TRUE)) {
  devtools::install_github("ScottCoffin/ToMEx2.0_EcoToxRisk", upgrade = "never", subdir = "package", build_vignettes = FALSE)
```
